- In light and high contrast they equal the brand and danger colours. In dark mode they are a step darker: the dark brand colour is light enough to read as text, and white on it falls below 4.5:1.

The values are not repeated here: the primitives are in `tokens.json` of @luz-ds/tokens, and every custom property of a package, with the file that declares it, is in the `properties` of its `classes.json`.

## Color
URL: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/tokens/color/
Files: src/semantic.css

Every colour a component may use, named by its job, with its value in light, dark and high contrast side by side.

Pick a token by its job, not by its colour. The name stays the same in every mode; the value changes.

- **Surfaces** for backgrounds, **text** for words, **lines** for borders and dividers.
- **Brand** for links and the main action; the **fill** tokens behind white text.
- **Status** for success, warning, danger and information, and nothing else.
- **Sidebar**, **inputs** and **code syntax** for those components only.

Each token shows its job, then its value in light, dark and high contrast, side by side. One click on a name selects all of it, ready to copy. In Figma the same names are variables: see [Tokens in Figma](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/tokens/figma/).

**All 55 semantic tokens, in 9 groups**

The values are not repeated here: the primitives are in `tokens.json` of @luz-ds/tokens, and every custom property of a package, with the file that declares it, is in the `properties` of its `classes.json`.

## Spacing and sizing
URL: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/tokens/spacing/
Files: tokens.json → spacing

The space scale for gaps and padding, and the heights of buttons and fields.

Take every gap, padding and margin from this scale, so spacing lines up across components. Use the smaller steps inside a component and the larger ones between sections.

A 2px hairline, then the unit `--luz-space-unit` (0.25rem, 4px at a 16px root) times 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 16 and 24: each power of two and its 1.5× half step. The unit is in rem, so spacing follows the font size the reader sets in the browser, as text does. Set it on `:root` to change the whole scale; components read the steps, never the unit.

### Control heights

`tokens.json → control`

44px is the WCAG 2.5.5 target size; the other steps are about 1.25× apart on the 4px grid.

- `--luz-control-sm`: close buttons and other small icon targets.
- `--luz-control-md`: small buttons.
- `--luz-control-lg`: buttons and fields, the default.
- `--luz-control-xl`: large buttons.

The values are not repeated here: the primitives are in `tokens.json` of @luz-ds/tokens, and every custom property of a package, with the file that declares it, is in the `properties` of its `classes.json`.

## Typography
URL: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/tokens/typography/

The three font stacks, the type scale in rem, and the smallest size each kind of text may use.

Two knobs size the whole scale. Set them on `:root`, in rem, in CSS of your own; a knob set on `body` or on a section changes nothing. Components read the `--luz-text-*` steps, never the knobs.

### Font roles

These four ship with core, not with tokens.

### Type scale and minimum sizes

Every size is in `rem`, so text follows the font size the reader sets in the browser, not only page zoom (WCAG 1.4.4). The scale is the same at every viewport width: no breakpoint makes text smaller. Above the 16px base each step is the one before times 1.25, rounded to 1/16 rem (a whole pixel at the default); below it are the readability floors. The Formula column is the chain as the stylesheet writes it; a browser that has `round()` rounds each step to 1/16 rem, which gives the Value column.

- **Body text** is `--luz-text-body` (17px at the defaults), with a line height of 1.6.
- **Secondary and UI text** is never below `--luz-text-sm` (14px).
- **Nothing** goes below `--luz-text-xs` (12px). Sizes relative to their context (`kbd`, `time`, `output`, inline code, captions) are clamped with `max()` so they cannot fall below the floor inside small text.
- **Form fields** use `--luz-text-control` (core setting): `--luz-text-md` on desktop, `max(1rem, var(--luz-text-base))` at 768px and below and on touch screens, never under 16px, where iOS Safari zooms the page into any smaller field.

The values are not repeated here: the primitives are in `tokens.json` of @luz-ds/tokens, and every custom property of a package, with the file that declares it, is in the `properties` of its `classes.json`.

## Color modes and themes
URL: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/tokens/modes/

Switch between light, dark and high contrast with one attribute, or make a look of your own.

Same markup, one attribute. Set `data-theme` on `<html>`, or on any element to scope a mode to it.

### Modes and themes

A color mode changes how light or dark the page is; a theme changes its whole identity. LUZ ships one look, in three modes. A theme of your own sits on top of it.

- The three modes ship with the tokens: `data-theme="light"`, `"dark"` and `"high-contrast"`. Light is the default, whatever the device's setting: [follow it with one script](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/tokens/modes/#system).
- The default look is Vejer, inspired by Vejer de la Frontera. It is the value the tokens have, not a file you load: ET Book for running text and headings, whitewash and sandstone surfaces, iron-black text, sky-blue links and actions, and every link underlined.
- LUZ ships no theme file. [Make your own](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/tokens/themes/): copy the template, change what you need, and check it.

Mode examples
```html
<html data-theme="dark">
<html data-theme="high-contrast">
<html data-theme="my-brand" data-mode="dark">
```

Every mode is measured against the same minimums: 4.5:1 for text, 3:1 for disabled text, borders and focus rings. The same measure runs on a theme of your own with `npx @luz-ds/tokens check-contrast`, or in the browser with [the contrast check](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/tokens/contrast/).

### Following the system or the clock

A page is light until it says otherwise: LUZ reads nothing of the visitor's device by itself. To start in dark when the device is in dark, set the attribute from a script in the head.

Following the system color mode
```html
<script>
  (function () {
    var mode;
    try { mode = localStorage.getItem("luz-theme"); } catch (e) {}
    if (["light", "dark", "high-contrast"].indexOf(mode) < 0) {
      mode = matchMedia("(prefers-contrast: more)").matches ? "high-contrast"
        : matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches ? "dark" : "light";
    }
    document.documentElement.dataset.theme = mode;
  })();
</script>
```

- Put it in `<head>`. It runs before the first paint, so the page does not flash light. Make it `<script type="module">` to keep it off the critical path: the page then paints light first, and switches.
- Under a CSP without `'unsafe-inline'`, serve it as a classic file in `<head>` or allow it by its `'sha256-…'` hash.
- A mode the reader chose wins. The color mode switcher stores it under `luz-theme`, and the script reads that first. The system setting is never stored, so the page keeps following it until the reader chooses.
- Without JavaScript the page stays light, and the radios of the switcher still change the mode for the session.
- It reads the setting once, when the page loads. To follow a change while the page is open, listen to the `change` event of `matchMedia()` and call `applyTheme(mode, { persist: false })` from `@luz-ds/core/theme`, only while `getStoredTheme()` is `null`.
- It sets the three modes. A theme of your own is set with `data-theme` and `data-mode`, as [the themes page](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/tokens/themes/) says.

The script sets the mode once. To keep following the system while the page is open, and to give the reader an Auto choice beside the three modes, wrap the switcher in [`<luz-mode>`](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/site/mode/), from `@luz-ds/site`.

- Auto follows the system: `prefers-contrast: more` gives high contrast, then `prefers-color-scheme: dark` gives dark, otherwise light.
- With `by="clock"` Auto follows the time of day instead, and writes the phase as `data-light`: see [how it works](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/site/mode/#how).
- A mode the reader chooses wins over both. Without JavaScript Auto is light.

The values are not repeated here: the primitives are in `tokens.json` of @luz-ds/tokens, and every custom property of a package, with the file that declares it, is in the `properties` of its `classes.json`.

## Radius
URL: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/tokens/radius/
Files: tokens.json → radius

The corner radius scale: square, 2px, 4px at most, and round.

Every box has the same corner, `--luz-radius-md` (4px): buttons, fields with a full border, cards, alerts, menus, dialogs. It is the ceiling: no rectangle is rounder. `--luz-radius-sm` is for small marks (inline code, `kbd`, a checkbox, a thin bar) and for a row inside a rounded box, so the two corners stay concentric. `--luz-radius-none` is for a box that joins a neighbour, or a field drawn by its bottom edge only, such as the select and the text field.

`--luz-radius-full` is not a corner: it makes a pill or a circle, for shapes that are round by nature, such as the switch track and the count badge. A dot, a radio button or a slider thumb is a circle with `50%`.

The values are not repeated here: the primitives are in `tokens.json` of @luz-ds/tokens, and every custom property of a package, with the file that declares it, is in the `properties` of its `classes.json`.

## Shadows
URL: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/tokens/shadows/
Files: tokens.json → shadow

The elevation scale: how far a surface seems to float above the page.

The higher the surface, the larger the shadow. Never use a shadow as the only edge of a surface: pair it with a border, because shadows disappear in forced colors.

The values below are the light ones. In dark mode the small, medium and large shadows are redrawn heavier, with a black of 40, 50 and 60 percent, because a pale shadow does not show on a dark surface. In high contrast they are replaced by outlines: the small shadow is none, the medium one is a 1px black line and the large one a 2px black line, since a blur is invisible there. `--luz-shadow-icon` is written once, so every mode reads the same value.

- `--luz-shadow-sm`: a card under the pointer.
- `--luz-shadow-md`: tooltips and toasts.
- `--luz-shadow-lg`: dialogs and the drawer.
- `--luz-shadow-icon`: an icon over a picture, such as the play button on a video.

The values are not repeated here: the primitives are in `tokens.json` of @luz-ds/tokens, and every custom property of a package, with the file that declares it, is in the `properties` of its `classes.json`.

## Motion
URL: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/tokens/motion/
Files: settings/_settings.css

The durations and easings of every transition, which drop to zero when the reader asks for reduced motion. Ships with @luz-ds/core.

Take every duration from a token. Under `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` all the durations become `0s`, so motion stops everywhere with no extra CSS.

Ships with core, not with tokens.

A transition with motion tokens
```css
.panel {
  transition: opacity var(--luz-duration-base) var(--luz-easing-standard);
}
```

- **Standard** for movement within the page, **enter** for things that arrive, **exit** for things that leave.
- **Spring** overshoots a little: keep it for small, playful details.
- Never hard-code a duration: it would ignore reduced motion.

The values are not repeated here: the primitives are in `tokens.json` of @luz-ds/tokens, and every custom property of a package, with the file that declares it, is in the `properties` of its `classes.json`.

## Layers
URL: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/tokens/layers/
Files: settings/_settings.css

Which layer sits on top: the z-index of every overlay, in order. Ships with @luz-ds/core.

### Z-index scale

Ships with core, not with tokens.

- Use the z-index tokens instead of numbers, so layers stay in this order.

The values are not repeated here: the primitives are in `tokens.json` of @luz-ds/tokens, and every custom property of a package, with the file that declares it, is in the `properties` of its `classes.json`.

## Layout and breakpoints
URL: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/tokens/layout/
Files: settings/_settings.css

How wide content gets, and where the layout changes. Ships with @luz-ds/core.

Ships with core, not with tokens.

- Breakpoints are reference values: media queries cannot read custom properties, so write the number, such as `@media (max-width: 768px)`.
- Safari on a Mac with always-visible scrollbars does not count the scrollbar in width media queries (WebKit bug 52653), so a breakpoint is crossed when the window is up to about 15 px wider than its value.

The values are not repeated here: the primitives are in `tokens.json` of @luz-ds/tokens, and every custom property of a package, with the file that declares it, is in the `properties` of its `classes.json`.

## Color palette
URL: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/tokens/palette/
Files: tokens.json → color

The primitive colour scales. For theme authors only: components never use them.

Building a component? Use the [semantic colours](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/tokens/color/) instead. These scales are what a theme points the semantic tokens at.

Raw values, never used directly in components. LUZ's own palette: `scripts/build-palette.js` computes every step in OKLCH from one lightness curve shared by all families, a chroma curve and a hue per family.

The values are not repeated here: the primitives are in `tokens.json` of @luz-ds/tokens, and every custom property of a package, with the file that declares it, is in the `properties` of its `classes.json`.

## Contrast check
URL: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/tokens/contrast/
Files: bin/luz-tokens.js

Check your own color overrides against the contrast LUZ promises, with one command or in the page, before they reach a user.

### Run it

LUZ keeps its own colors readable in light, dark and high contrast. The moment you override a token, that promise is yours. `check-contrast` reads the `--luz-*` declarations of your stylesheet, puts them over LUZ's tokens as the browser would, and measures the same pairs the component pages list. It needs Node 20 or later and nothing else. `luz-check`, the command of [@luz-ds/check](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/get-started/ai/), runs the same check on the stylesheets you name, next to its rules for the HTML and CSS of a page.

The command
```text
npx @luz-ds/tokens check-contrast my-theme.css
```

Name your files in the order the page loads them. Use `--json` for a machine-readable report, and `--strict` to make the warnings fail too.

Example output
```text
✗ light, high-contrast: --luz-text-secondary on surface-page is 2.8:1, needs 4.5:1 (text)
    --luz-text-secondary: #999 is set in my-theme.css:2
✗ contrast: 5 pairs fail (9 of 378 measurements) in light, dark, high-contrast
```

### What it checks

WCAG 2.x relative luminance, the contrast of WCAG 2.2 level AA. APCA is not used, because it is not part of the standard.

Pairs are checked in light, dark and high contrast, and in each `[data-theme="name"]` your file defines, as `name` and `name/light`, `name/dark` and `name/high-contrast`. Translucent colors are placed over the surface below them, as in the page. A *warning* is an aim LUZ sets itself, stricter than WCAG, such as the fill of a checked box against the page: it is shown and never fails the check unless you pass `--strict`.

### What it reads

- **Selectors:** `:root`, `html`, `[data-theme="x"]` and `[data-mode="y"]`, alone or together. A later rule wins over an earlier one of the same specificity, and a more specific selector wins over a later one. A `:root` override, loaded after LUZ, also reaches dark and high contrast unless that mode sets the token again: set a token per mode.
- **At-rules:** `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` and `light`, and `@layer` and `@supports`, taken as true. The order of layers is not modeled.
- **Values:** `#rgb`, `#rrggbb` with or without alpha, `rgb()` and `hsl()` in either syntax, `white`, `black`, `transparent`, and `var()` chains.
- **Everything else is reported, not skipped:** a class selector, another media query or a rule it did not understand is listed as ignored. A color it cannot read, such as `color-mix()` or `oklch()`, counts as a failure, because a pair that was not measured is not a pair that passed.

### Exit codes

### In your build

The command fails the step on a failure, so one line is enough.

A package.json script
```json
{
  "scripts": {
    "check:contrast": "luz-tokens check-contrast src/theme.css"
  }
}
```

### Try it in the page

With JavaScript on, you can paste your overrides here and run the same check. Nothing leaves the page. Without it, use the command above: it does the same.

The values are not repeated here: the primitives are in `tokens.json` of @luz-ds/tokens, and every custom property of a package, with the file that declares it, is in the `properties` of its `classes.json`.

## Make your own theme
URL: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/tokens/themes/
Files: themes/_template.css

LUZ ships one look in three color modes. A theme of your own is a file of semantic tokens: start from the template, check it, load it.

### What a theme is

A **color mode** says how light or dark the page is: `light`, `dark` or `high-contrast`. A **theme** is a whole identity: colors, and optionally the fonts, radii and shadows. Every theme has the three modes.

- LUZ ships **one look**, Vejer, in the three modes. It is the default: with no attribute you get its light mode.
- A theme of your own overrides **semantic tokens** only. It never changes a primitive, and it never touches a component's CSS.
- You name it with `data-theme` and pick its mode with `data-mode`.
- Overriding tokens and making a theme are the same thing: a theme is a named set of overrides, with a mode for each of its looks.

### Make one, step by step

1. **Copy the template.** It is `@luz-ds/core/themes/_template.css`. Every value in it is LUZ's own, so it passes the contrast check before you change anything.
2. **Rename it.** Replace `my-brand`, three times, by the name of your theme: lowercase letters, digits and hyphens.
3. **Change what you need.** Start with the brand colors and the surfaces. Keep the three blocks complete: a token left out of the dark block takes its light value.
4. **Check it.** Run the command in [Check it](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/tokens/themes/#check) until it passes.
5. **Load it** after `luz-tokens.css` and `luz.css`, and set the attribute.
6. **List it** in `data-luz-themes`, so the mode switcher remembers the visitor's choice.

Loading a theme
```html
<link rel="stylesheet" href="luz-tokens.css">
<link rel="stylesheet" href="luz.css">
<link rel="stylesheet" href="my-brand.css">

<html lang="en" data-theme="my-brand" data-luz-themes="my-brand">
<!-- or, in its dark mode -->
<html lang="en" data-theme="my-brand" data-mode="dark" data-luz-themes="my-brand">
```

A small theme can be only the tokens that differ, in the first block: what you leave out takes LUZ's value. Fill the dark and high-contrast blocks as well if you offer those modes.

A minimal theme
```css
[data-theme="my-brand"] {
  --luz-brand-primary: #0057ff;
  --luz-brand-hover: #0043c2;
  --luz-brand-active: #003399;
  --luz-brand-fill: #0057ff;
  --luz-focus-ring: #0057ff;
  --luz-surface-page: #f8faff;
}
```

### The tokens a theme sets

The template names all of them, in each of its three blocks. They are the same tokens as the [color page](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/tokens/color/), with the job of each; this is the list, by group.

**Optional, and not in the three blocks:** `--luz-font-body`, `--luz-font-heading` and `--luz-font-serif` for the fonts, `--luz-radius-sm` and `-md` for the corners, and `--luz-shadow-sm`, `-md` and `-lg`. Set them in the first block.

**Not in a theme:** the sizes (`--luz-type-base`, `--luz-type-ratio` and `--luz-space-unit`) are set on `:root`, not in a theme. A theme changes colours per mode; the sizes are one page-wide choice. See [Typography](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/tokens/typography/) and [Spacing](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/tokens/spacing/).

### Check it

The command
```text
npx @luz-ds/tokens check-contrast my-brand.css
```

- It reads the theme as the browser would: the first block is the light mode, and each `data-mode` block lays on top of it.
- The minimums are 4.5:1 for text, 3:1 for disabled text, borders, field borders and focus rings, in all three modes. Exit code `1` when a pair fails.
- You can also paste the theme into [the contrast check](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/tokens/contrast/) in the page.
- **LUZ guarantees only what it ships.** Your theme is as accessible as this check says, and no more.

### Layers, modes and scope

- **Layers.** Put the theme in `@layer luz.themes` to keep it below your own CSS, or leave it unlayered to win over all of LUZ. Either way it wins over `luz.tokens`. [The layers page](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/get-started/layers/) has the order.
- **One zone.** `data-theme` works on any element: the theme applies to that element and what is inside it. A date or time picker and a select take their color scheme from an ancestor `data-theme`, so for those put the attribute on `<html>`.
- **Forced colors.** A reader who forces colors sees system colors, not your theme. Nothing to do: the components handle it.
- **Print.** The `luz.print` layer sets paper colors whatever the theme.
- **The OS preference.** With no stored choice and no attribute, the page is light. To follow `prefers-color-scheme`, [set `data-theme` from a short script](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/tokens/modes/#system): it is on the color modes page.

### Limits

- One theme at a time on an element. Mix a theme and a mode, not two themes.
- The mode switcher knows only the names in `data-luz-themes`: a name that is not listed works as an attribute, and is not remembered.
- `light-dark()` is not used: it is not Baseline Widely available before 2026-11-13.

The values are not repeated here: the primitives are in `tokens.json` of @luz-ds/tokens, and every custom property of a package, with the file that declares it, is in the `properties` of its `classes.json`.

How LUZ styles each of the 116 current HTML elements, with a live example and the markup to copy.

## Forms
URL: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/html/forms/

Controls and the structure around them. Fields, selects and buttons get their look from a .luz-* class; textarea, output, meter and progress are styled with no class.

- `<button>`
- `<datalist>`
- `<fieldset>`
- `<form>`
- `<input>`
- `<label>`
- `<legend>`
- `<meter>`
- `<optgroup>`
- `<option>`
- `<output>`
- `<progress>`
- `<select>`
- `<selectedcontent>`
- `<textarea>`
- The 22 input types

## Components
URL: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/

Every core component, grouped by task, with a live example, the markup to copy and when to use it.

Level 2 · @luz-ds/core

Every core component, grouped by task, with a live example, the markup to copy and when to use it.

A **component** is one reusable piece, almost always tied to one HTML element: a button, a field, a table. A **pattern** combines components to do a product task, such as a page shell or a site search; patterns are in [Site](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/site/).

## Accordion
URL: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/accordion/
Example: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/examples/components/accordion.html
Files: components/accordion.css · Package: @luz-ds/core

Shows and hides sections of content with the native details and summary elements, one at a time if you name the group.

### Known issues
Two points to know before you rely on a named group.

**Exclusive group.** The `name` attribute works in Chrome and Edge 120, Safari 17.2 and Firefox 130, all from September 2024 or earlier, so it is not yet Baseline widely available. In an older browser each panel opens on its own: nothing is lost.

**Screen readers.** How NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver, TalkBack and Orca announce an exclusive group has not been tested for LUZ, and no support data was checked. The grouping of an exclusive set is not described to assistive technology: the HTML accessibility mapping for it is still an open issue (see the [Open UI explainer](https://open-ui.org/components/accordion.explainer)).

### Copy the markup
Accordion markup
```html
<div class="luz-accordion">
  <details name="faq" open>
    <summary>What is a design token?</summary>
    <p>A named value that components read.</p>
  </details>
  <details name="faq">
    <summary>Does it need JavaScript?</summary>
    <p>No.</p>
  </details>
</div>
```

### Variants and options
A single `<details>` needs no class: the elements layer styles it. The class only joins a stack.

- `.luz-accordion`: Joins the `<details>` inside it into one block: one edge between them, rounded corners only on the block
- `name="…"`: Connects the details with the same name: only one is open at a time. They need not be adjacent
- `open`: Starts a panel open. In a named group, only the first `open` one in the source stays open

### How it works
Native `<details>` and `<summary>`, styled by `elements/interactive.css` with no class. `components/accordion.css` adds only the joined block. No JavaScript.

- The summary is the label of the panel; the rest of the details is its content.
- Closed content is not shown and is out of the reading order until the panel opens.

### Without JavaScript
Nothing changes: opening, closing and grouping are the browser's. The accordion is complete without a script.

### Keyboard and ARIA
Tab reaches each summary in order. Enter or Space opens or closes it. There are no arrow-key shortcuts between panels.

- Add no role: a `<details>` already has its semantics, and no ARIA role is allowed on it.
- Keep links and buttons out of the summary: it is itself the control.

### When to use
Use an accordion for content that most readers can skip, grouped under short titles.

- Frequently asked questions and long reference lists.
- Optional detail under a short answer.

### When not to use
Do not hide what every reader needs, and do not use it to move around the site.

- For the main sections of a site, use a [sidebar](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/sidebar/). For content a reader switches between, use [tabs](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/tabs/).
- Do not put an error, a warning or a required step inside a closed panel.
- With only one or two short answers, show them as plain text.

### Do and don't
- **Do** Give each summary a short title that says what the panel answers.
- **Don't** Use a whole sentence of context as the title: it hides the point and wraps.

### Writing the content
- Write the summary as the question or the topic, in sentence case, in a few words.
- Put the answer first in the panel. Keep it short; link to a page for more.
- Order the panels as readers ask: most common first.

## Alert
URL: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/alert/
Example: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/examples/components/alert.html
Files: components/alert.css · Package: @luz-ds/core

Tells the reader about the page or a task: information, success, a warning or an error.

### Known issues
None known.

### Copy the markup
Warning alert markup
```html
<div class="luz-alert luz-alert--warning">
  <div class="luz-alert__icon" aria-hidden="true">!</div>
  <div>
    <div class="luz-alert__title">Warning</div>
    <div class="luz-alert__body">Storage is almost full. Delete old builds to free space.</div>
  </div>
</div>
```

### Variants and options
One modifier sets the status. Write the status in the title too: the colour is only a second cue.

- `.luz-alert--info`: Something useful to know
- `.luz-alert--success`: A task that finished well
- `.luz-alert--warning`: Something that may go wrong soon
- `.luz-alert--error`: Something that went wrong and needs action

### How it works
A block with an icon, a title and a body, styled by `components/alert.css`. No JavaScript.

- The icon is decorative (`aria-hidden="true"`): the title already names the status.
- The start border and the title take the status colour; the body stays in the secondary text colour.

### Without JavaScript
Nothing changes: the alert is static HTML and CSS.

### Keyboard and ARIA
An alert is not interactive and takes no focus.

- An alert that is on the page when it loads needs no role.
- An alert that appears after an action must be announced: insert it into a container that is already on the page with `role="status"`, or `role="alert"` for an error that needs attention now.

### When to use
Use an alert to tell the reader about a state that matters on this page.

- Information they need before they act: "This project is archived."
- The result of a task: success, a warning or an error.

### When not to use
Do not use an alert for a message that must stop the reader, or one they can safely miss.

- A decision the reader must make before going on: use a [modal](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/modal/).
- A short confirmation that needs no action: use a [toast](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/toast/).
- An error on one field: put it next to the field ([form fields](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/form/)).
- More than two alerts at once: merge them, or the reader stops reading them.

### Do and don't
- **Do** Say what happened and what to do next: “Storage is almost full. Delete old builds or change your plan.”
- **Don't** “Something went wrong.” names neither what failed nor what the reader can do about it.

### Writing the content
Say what happened, then what to do next.

- The title is the status in one or two words: "Warning", "Build failed".
- The body is one or two short sentences: "The build failed. Check the log and run it again."
- Never rely on the colour or the icon alone.

## Avatar
URL: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/avatar/
Example: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/examples/components/avatar.html
Files: components/avatar.css · Package: @luz-ds/core

Shows who a person or a team is, with their initials or a photo, in three sizes.

### Known issues
If a photo does not load, the browser draws its `alt` text in the box, in the avatar's capitals; a long name can spill past the box. The name is still there for a screen reader.

### Copy the markup
Avatar markup
```html
<span class="luz-avatar luz-avatar--md" role="img" aria-label="Carlos Díaz">CD</span>
```

Next to the person's name, the avatar repeats it: hide it instead.

Avatar next to a name markup
```html
<span class="luz-avatar luz-avatar--sm" aria-hidden="true">CD</span> Carlos Díaz
```

With a photo: the image fills the box, cropped to a square.

Avatar with a photo markup
```html
<span class="luz-avatar luz-avatar--md"><img src="/img/ana.jpg" width="36" height="36" alt="Ana Belén"></span>

<span class="luz-avatar luz-avatar--lg"><img src="/img/ana.jpg" width="48" height="48" alt=""></span> Ana Belén
```

### Variants and options
Pick one size modifier. Without one, the avatar has no size of its own. The content is the initials or one `<img>`.

- `.luz-avatar--sm`: 24 × 24 px, extra-small text
- `.luz-avatar--md`: 36 × 36 px, small text
- `.luz-avatar--lg`: 48 × 48 px, base text
- `<img>` inside: A photo: fills the box, cropped to a square, with the avatar's corners

### How it works
An inline box that centres its text, styled by `components/avatar.css`. No JavaScript.

- The initials are set in the mono font, in capitals (`text-transform: uppercase`).
- The colours are the brand tint and the brand text colour, in every mode.
- A photo is an `<img>` at `100%` of the box with `object-fit: cover` and the corners of the avatar (`border-radius: inherit`). The box does not clip (no `overflow: hidden`), so initials that outgrow a small box at 200 % text stay readable.

### Without JavaScript
Nothing changes: the avatar is HTML and CSS only.

### Keyboard and ARIA
An avatar is not interactive and takes no focus.

- Initials on their own are an image: `role="img"` and an `aria-label` with the full name, so a screen reader does not spell out the initials.
- A photo on its own is named by its `alt`, with the person's name: no role, no `aria-label`. When the photo is all there is in a link or a button, the `alt` names the control, so it says the action too: `alt="Ana Belén, your account"`.
- Next to the name, an avatar is decoration: `aria-hidden="true"` on initials, `alt=""` on a photo.
- Inside a link or a button with text, the control's text names it; hide the avatar.

### When to use
Use an avatar to identify a person or an account where space is tight, such as a list of members or the author of a comment.

### When not to use
Do not use an avatar as the only way to tell people apart.

- Two people can share initials: show the name as text nearby.
- For a status or a category, use a [tag](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/tag/).
- For the portrait of a speaker or a product, a size of its own, use a card with the image frame: see [Speakers](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/landing/templates/#speakers) in the landing page templates. An avatar is 24 to 48 px.

### Do and don't
- **Do** Show the name next to the avatar: two people can share initials.
- **Don't** Avatars alone, as the only way to tell people apart: “AB” and “AB” are two different people.
- **Do** Give every photo in a list the same framing: head and shoulders, the face away from the edges, because the box crops it to a square.
- **Don't** Mix photos with initials in a list that could be all one or the other: the people without a photo look like a different kind of member.

### Writing the content
Two initials, from the name the person uses.

- The accessible name is the full name, never the initials. For a photo, that is its `alt`.
- Use the same size for every avatar in one list.

## Band
URL: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/band/
Example: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/examples/components/band.html
Files: components/band.css · Package: @luz-ds/core

Sets one block of a page on a tint that runs from edge to edge, while its content keeps the column.

### Known issues
The band has three, all from the way it draws the tint.

- **A tooltip at its top edge is clipped.** The band cuts off whatever sticks out above or below it. A CSS tooltip on a control that is the first thing in a band is cut at 200 percent text and larger. Start the band with its heading, and keep tooltips off the first control. Dropdown menus and other popovers are not clipped.
- **Outline and ghost buttons.** Their hover colour is the band's own tint, so the hover shows no change. The label and the outline still identify them. Use one primary button, and an outline button for a second way.
- **Forced colors.** The tint is removed, so the band is its heading, text and buttons between two thin rules in the system text colour.

### Copy the markup
Band markup
```html
<main id="main-content" class="o-container o-stack">
  <!-- other sections -->
  <section class="o-stack luz-band" aria-labelledby="last-seats-title">
    <h2 id="last-seats-title">Registration closes on 30 April</h2>
    <p>The hall holds 400 people, and the Two days ticket sold out last year.</p>
    <div class="o-actions">
      <a class="luz-btn luz-btn--primary" href="/register/">Register now</a>
    </div>
  </section>
</main>
```

### Variants and options
There are no variants: one class on any block. The layout inside is yours: `.o-stack` above spaces its children.

- `.luz-band`: The block on a `--luz-brand-subtle` tint that runs from edge to edge of the page, with 48 px (`--luz-space-2xl`) above and below its content. The content keeps the page's column

### How it works
CSS from `@luz-ds/core`. No JavaScript.

- The band stays inside the page's column, so its text keeps the column's start edge. The tint is a `box-shadow` that spreads past the block, cut off above and below by `clip-path`. A shadow adds no scrollable width; `100vw` would, whenever the page has a scrollbar. In an `.o-shell` the tint stops at `.o-main`.
- Any block can be a band: a `<section>` with its heading, or a plain `<div>`.
- Put it on the page itself, inside the main column. Inside a card or an element with its own background the tint is drawn over that surface, and it runs out of the element when that element is wider than the window.

### Without JavaScript
Nothing changes: the band is CSS.

### Keyboard and ARIA
The band has no interaction, and adds no role.

- A `<section>` named with `aria-labelledby` becomes a region landmark; a `<div>` band is just a block.
- The tint carries no meaning, and it is not what groups the band: the section and its heading are. Without the tint (forced colors, print) the grouping stays.
- Controls inside the band keep their own focus ring. The 48 px above and below leaves room for it at 200 percent text and at 320 px wide.

### When to use
Use a band for a call to act near the end of a long page, or for one pause in the middle of it.

### When not to use
Do not band every section: when everything stands out, nothing does.

- One band for each screen height at most; two in a row read as a new background, not as a call to act.
- Do not use the tint to say something (a warning, a status): it carries no meaning, and forced colors remove it. Use an [alert](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/alert/).
- Do not put a band inside a card or on a `--luz-surface` area, or around the whole page. In dark mode the primary button falls to 2.7:1 against a tint laid over `--luz-surface`, under the 3:1 a control's edge needs.
- Do not put a `.luz-btn--secondary` on the band: its fill is the tint's own colour, and it reads as plain text.

### Do and don't
- **Do** One band, with a heading that says why now and one primary button.
- **Don't** Two bands in a row: the second reads as a new background, and neither stands out as the call to act.

### Writing the content
On a band, the heading says why now, not the action: "Registration closes on 30 April", not "Register".

- Add one sentence of support, one primary button and, if you need a second way, one outline button.

## Breadcrumb
URL: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/breadcrumb/
Example: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/examples/components/breadcrumb.html
Files: components/breadcrumb.css · Package: @luz-ds/core

Shows where the page sits in the site, as a trail of links to its parents.

### Known issues
None known.

### Copy the markup
Breadcrumb markup
```html
<nav aria-label="Breadcrumb">
  <ol class="luz-breadcrumb">
    <li><a class="luz-breadcrumb__item" href="/">Home</a></li>
    <li><a class="luz-breadcrumb__item" href="/settings/">Settings</a></li>
    <li><span class="luz-breadcrumb__item" aria-current="page">Billing</span></li>
  </ol>
</nav>
```

### Variants and options
There are no modifiers. The separator is drawn by the CSS between two items: there is nothing to write for it.

- `.luz-breadcrumb`: The ordered list: one row of items, which wraps onto more lines when it is narrow. Each `<li>` after the first starts with a slash
- `.luz-breadcrumb__item`: A parent link, or the current page as text
- `aria-current="page"`: Marks the current page: primary text colour and medium weight

### How it works
The [APG breadcrumb pattern](https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/breadcrumb/): a `<nav>` landmark around an ordered list of links, styled by `components/breadcrumb.css`. No JavaScript.

- The list is ordered because the order is the meaning: screen readers announce a list and its number of items.
- The current page is the last item, a `<span>` with `aria-current="page"`, not a link to itself.
- The separator is a border drawn by `::before` with empty content, so assistive technology has nothing to read.

### Without JavaScript
Nothing changes: the breadcrumb is a list of links and CSS. Without CSS it reads as a numbered list.

### Keyboard and ARIA
Tab reaches each parent link in order; Enter follows it. The current page is not in the tab order.

- Name the `<nav>` "Breadcrumb" with `aria-label`, so it differs from the main navigation.
- `aria-current="page"` tells screen readers which item is the current page.

### When to use
Use a breadcrumb when pages sit three or more levels deep, so the reader sees where they are and can go up a level.

### When not to use
Do not use a breadcrumb on a flat site, or as the only navigation.

- For the main sections of a site, use a [sidebar](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/sidebar/) or a header navigation.
- For steps in a process, show the step number in the page heading instead.

### Do and don't
- **Do** Use the titles of the pages, and end with the current page as text.
- **Don't** Internal names (“UI kit”, “luz-btn”) instead of the titles the reader saw on the way.

### Writing the content
Use the title of each page, shortened if it is long.

- Start at the home or the top of the section.
- End with the current page, as text, not as a link.

## Button
URL: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/button/
Example: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/examples/components/button.html
Files: components/button.css · Package: @luz-ds/core

Starts an action on the current page, such as saving, sending or opening a dialog.

### Known issues
None known.

### Copy the markup
Primary button markup
```html
<button class="luz-btn luz-btn--primary" type="button">Save changes</button>
```

A link that goes somewhere, with the look of a button:

Link styled as a button markup
```html
<a class="luz-btn luz-btn--outline" href="/pricing/">See the plans</a>
```

The full width of a narrow container, such as a card or a form on a phone:

Full-width button markup
```html
<form action="/cart/add" method="post">
  <button class="luz-btn luz-btn--primary luz-btn--block" type="submit">Add to cart</button>
</form>
```

### Variants and options
Combine `.luz-btn` with one variant and, if needed, one size and the full width.

- `.luz-btn--primary`: Brand fill: the main action of the view
- `.luz-btn--secondary`: Strong neutral surface: a second action
- `.luz-btn--outline`: Brand text and border, no fill
- `.luz-btn--ghost`: Brand text only: a low-priority action
- `.luz-btn--danger`: Danger fill: an action that deletes or cannot be undone
- `.luz-btn--sm`: 36 px high, small text
- `.luz-btn--lg`: 56 px high, base text
- `.luz-btn--block`: Fills the width of its container, and its label wraps: for a card, a form or a drawer, not for a wide column
- `disabled`: Muted text, dashed border, no pointer events

The default height is 44 px. An `<svg>` inside the button is drawn at 16 × 16 px, before or after the label.

### How it works
A native `<button>` (or `<a>`) with classes from `components/button.css`. No JavaScript.

- Set `type="button"` unless the button submits a form; the default type is `submit`.
- The height is a minimum: the label can grow with the reader's font size.
- `.luz-btn--block` sets `inline-size: 100%`. Put it where the button is the only thing in its row: in a flex row it would take the whole row. Its label wraps, and a word longer than the box breaks, so nothing leaves the button at 320 px or at 200 % text.

### Without JavaScript
A button works like any native button: it submits its form or runs nothing. What it does on click is up to your script.

### Keyboard and ARIA
Tab reaches the button; Enter or Space presses it. A link styled as a button answers to Enter only, as every link does.

- No ARIA is needed: the visible label is the name.
- An icon-only button needs a name: `aria-label="Close"`, and the icon `aria-hidden="true"`.
- A disabled button is skipped by Tab and screen readers may not find it: prefer an enabled button that explains what is missing.

### When to use
Use a button to start an action on the current page: save, send, delete, open a dialog.

- One primary button per view, for the action most people take.
- Secondary, outline or ghost buttons for the other actions.
- The full width (`.luz-btn--block`) when the action is the only thing in a narrow container: a card, a drawer, the submit of a form on a phone.

### When not to use
Do not use a button to go to another page: use a link, styled as a button only when it is the main call to action.

- For several related actions in a row, use an [action group](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/layout/#objects-actions).
- Do not disable a button to hide an action the reader cannot take yet: say why instead.
- Do not stretch a button across a wide column: a bar 1,000 px wide is not a button. Two actions side by side are two buttons of their own width.

### Do and don't
- **Do** One primary button, for the action most people take; the others are quieter.
- **Don't** Two primary buttons: neither one reads as the next step, so the reader has to stop and compare.

### Writing the content
Start with a verb and say the result: "Save changes", "Delete draft".

- Never "OK", "Submit" or "Click here".
- Sentence case, two or three words, no full stop.
- Use the same words for the same action everywhere.
- A full-width bar invites a long label: keep it under about 24 characters, or let it wrap.

## Card
URL: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/card/
Example: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/examples/components/card.html
Files: components/card.css · Package: @luz-ds/core

Groups a few facts about one thing on a bordered surface.

### Known issues
In a linked card, the body text, the price included, cannot be selected with a mouse: the title link covers the whole card, so a drag follows or moves the link. Find in page, keyboard selection and screen readers reach the text as usual.

### Copy the markup
Card markup
```html
<article class="luz-card">
  <h3 class="luz-card__title">Database</h3>
  <p class="luz-card__body">48 active connections.</p>
</article>
```

### Variants and options
One card, four classes and one modifier. A link in the title makes the whole card one link; any other link or button in it is raised above that link.

- `.luz-card`: The surface: border, rounded corners and padding
- `.luz-card__title`: Base size, semibold, primary text colour
- `.luz-card__body`: Medium size, secondary text colour
- `.luz-card__price`: The price: base size, semibold, primary text colour, figures of equal width. A previous price goes in `<s>`
- `.luz-card--featured`: The one card to look at first in a group: a 2 px border in the brand colour, as tall as its neighbours. Say why in words too, with a tag such as “Most chosen”
- `<a>` in `.luz-card__title`: A linked card: the link covers the card, the title turns sans, a darker border and a shadow on hover, a focus ring round the card

Compose a card with the layout objects and the other components, with no new class: a linked card, an avatar or an icon beside the text with `.o-media`, an image on top, and a row of actions with `.o-row`.

- **Linked card:** the `<a>` goes inside the heading, round its text. A second link or a button in it is allowed, and sits above the title link: see Product card below.
- **Avatar or icon:** `.o-media` puts it beside `.o-media__body`, which holds the title and the body. Next to a name, hide the avatar with `aria-hidden="true"`: it repeats the name.
- **Image on top:** the [image frame](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/image/) (`.luz-image`), inside the padding, with `.u-mb-sm` under it. Its alt text says what the picture shows; if it only repeats the title, leave it empty (`alt=""`).
- **Actions:** `.o-row` with small buttons (`.luz-btn--sm`) or tags (`.luz-tag`), last in the card. In a linked card, one action at most, as a button after the title.

#### Product card

A card for a shop is the card with an image, a linked title, a price and one action. The action is a button in a form, so it works without JavaScript; it is raised above the title link, so it takes its own click.

Product card markup
```html
<article>
  <h4 id="red-wines">Red wines</h4>
  <ul class="o-grid o-grid--auto" aria-labelledby="red-wines">
    <li class="luz-card">
      <div class="luz-image luz-image--4x3 u-mb-sm">
        <picture>…<img src="malbec.jpg" alt="" width="640" height="480" loading="lazy" decoding="async"></picture>
      </div>
      <h5 class="luz-card__title"><a href="/wines/malbec-2021/">Malbec 2021</a></h5>
      <p class="luz-card__body">Bodega Albar · 75 cl</p>
      <p class="luz-card__price"><data value="12.50">12,50 €</data></p>
      <form action="/cart/add" method="post">
        <input type="hidden" name="product" value="malbec-2021">
        <button class="luz-btn luz-btn--primary luz-btn--block" type="submit">Add to cart<span class="u-sr-only"> Malbec 2021</span></button>
      </form>
    </li>
  </ul>
  <output class="u-sr-only" id="cart-status"></output>
</article>
```

- **The button is the width of the card** with `.luz-btn--block`: a thumb finds it, and its label wraps and breaks inside the card at any text size.
- **One action, one link.** The name is the link; the button is the action. A card with a second action (a wish list, a comparison) has outgrown a card: send the reader to the product's own page.
- **The button's name is unique.** The visible words come first, then the product's name in `.u-sr-only`, repeating the link's text exactly (keep the space before it). A list of twelve buttons all called “Add to cart” says nothing to someone who lists the buttons of a page, or says them by voice.
- **The list is named by its heading:** `aria-labelledby` points at the `<h4>` above it, and the cards use the next level. Core styles no list: remove the bullets and the indent with your own rule (`list-style: none; margin: 0; padding: 0`).
- **The old price is `<s>`,** with the words “Now” and “Was” hidden visually so the order is clear to a screen reader; the line through it is not colour.
- **Feedback after a script adds the item:** keep an empty `<output>` (it has the role `status`) in the page from the start and write “Malbec 2021 added to the cart” into it; focus stays on the button. A status region that is created together with its text is often not announced. Without a script the form posts and the cart page is the feedback.
- **Sold out:** replace the form with `<span class="luz-tag">Sold out</span>`; do not disable the button.
- With core alone there is no image frame: use an `<img>` with your own size rules.

#### Featured card

In a group of plans or offers, `.luz-card--featured` marks the one to look at first. The class says nothing to a screen reader, so the card carries a tag with the reason, in its text.

Featured card markup
```html
<article class="luz-card luz-card--featured">
  <h4 class="luz-card__title">Two days</h4>
  <p class="luz-card__price"><data value="149">149 €</data></p>
  <p class="luz-card__body">Both days, lunch and the recordings.
    <span class="luz-tag luz-tag--blue">Most chosen</span></p>
  <a class="luz-btn luz-btn--primary luz-btn--block" href="/register/?ticket=two-days">Choose Two days</a>
</article>
```

- **One featured card per group.** If everything is featured, nothing is.
- **The words are required.** A 2 px border is a second cue for people who see it, and in forced colors the only one; a tag such as “Most chosen” or “Best value” is the one that reaches everybody. Put it in the body or beside the title.
- **It stays as tall as its neighbours:** the extra pixel of border is taken from the padding.

### How it works
A container styled by `components/card.css`. No JavaScript.

- Use any element: `<article>` for a self-contained item, `<div>` for a group of facts, `<li>` inside a list of cards.
- The title class goes on the heading level that fits the page outline.
- The corners are rounded with `--luz-radius-md`, like a figure or a dropdown.
- The last title or body has no space under it: the padding is the card's last space.
- A linked card: the link's `::after` is stretched over the card (`position: absolute; inset: 0`), so a click anywhere in it follows the link. The card is `position: relative` to hold it. Any other link or control inside the card (`a`, `button`, `input`, `select`, `textarea`, `summary`) is `position: relative` with `z-index: 1`, so it paints above that overlay and takes its own click; the title link is the one thing never raised. A button's label wraps in a card (`white-space: normal`), so a long label or enlarged text stays inside it. On hover the border turns `--luz-input-border` and a small shadow shows; on keyboard focus a ring goes round the card. The title of a linked card is in sans, as a nav or a list of links is; a card without a link keeps the heading face. Both are found with `:has()`; a card without a link does not change on hover.
- `.luz-card--featured` sets `border-width: 2px` in `--luz-brand-primary` and takes the extra pixel from the padding, so the card keeps the height of its neighbours. In a linked card the border turns `--luz-brand-hover` on hover, and the keyboard ring stands 4 px off the border, so it does not read as a thicker border.
- To lay cards out, use the [grid objects](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/layout/), such as the [split grid](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/layout/#objects-actions) for two cards side by side.

### Without JavaScript
Nothing changes: a card, linked or not, is HTML and CSS.

### Keyboard and ARIA
A card is not interactive and takes no focus.

- In a card that is not linked, links and buttons inside keep their own behaviour.
- A link or a button in a linked card is raised above the title link, so the pointer reaches it. It has its own tab stop, in source order, and its own ring; give each a name that is unique on the page (see Product card).
- A linked card has a tab stop for its title link and one for each other link or button. Enter follows the title link; Enter or Space presses a button. The ring shows round the title link and round the whole card; a button shows its own ring only.
- A screen reader names the link with the title, then reads the body as text. Add no `role`, `tabindex` or `aria-label` to the card.
- Put the link on the title text, never round the card: a link round the card takes every word in it as its name.

### When to use
Use a card to group a small set of facts that read as one unit, often in a grid of similar items.

- A featured card (`.luz-card--featured`) for the one recommended choice in a group of plans or offers.

### When not to use
Do not use a card to box content that is not a separate thing.

- For rows of records with the same attributes, use a [table](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/table/).
- For a message about the page, use an [alert](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/alert/).
- For a list of links, each with one line of description, use a plain list (`<ul>`): a card per link adds borders and nothing else.
- A card with more than one action besides its title link is a form or a page: use the page of the thing, not a card.
- Do not put a card inside a card.
- Do not feature several cards in a group, or use the border as the only cue: say why in words too.

### Do and don't
- **Do** Put the link on the title: the whole card takes the click and the link is named by the title. An action goes after it as a button, with a name of its own.
- **Don't** A link round the whole card, or a second link such as “Read more” in it: the first takes every word of the card as its name, the second sits under the title link and says nothing out of context.
- **Do** Feature one card, and say why in words: the border draws the eye, the tag tells everybody.
- **Don't** A featured card with no words: a reader who does not see the border, or the colour, gets no hint that it is the one to choose.

### Writing the content
A short noun as the title, then one or two lines.

- No full stop on the title.
- Keep cards in one group parallel: the same kind of title, the same length of body.
- In a linked card, the title is the link text: it says where the link goes, so the card needs no “Read more”.
- On a featured card, a tag of one to three words says why: “Most chosen”, “Best value”. A button names the plan: “Choose Two days”.
- A price with its currency, in the format of the page's language. A button says what it does and for what: “Add to cart”, then the product's name for assistive technology.

## Code
URL: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/code/
Example: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/examples/components/code.html
Files: components/code.css · Package: @luz-ds/core

Shows code inside a sentence, or in a block with syntax colours in every mode.

### Known issues
The highlighter is a set of patterns, not a parser: JSX tags, the contents of HTML `style` and `script` elements and unquoted attribute values stay plain. The colours are decoration only: assistive technology reads the code the same way.

### Copy the markup
Code block markup
```html
<pre class="luz-code-block" data-lang="css" tabindex="0" role="region" aria-label="Panel styles"><code>.panel {
  color: var(--luz-text-primary);
}</code></pre>
```

Inline code markup
```html
<p>Set the colour with <code class="luz-code-inline">--luz-text-primary</code>.</p>
```

Highlighting script code
```js
import { initHighlight } from "@luz-ds/core/highlight";
initHighlight();
```

### Variants and options
Two classes, and the language in an attribute.

- `.luz-code-block`: A block on the muted surface, mono font, scrolls sideways when a line is long
- `.luz-code-inline`: Code inside a sentence, in the code colour
- `data-lang`: The language: `html`, `css`, `js`, `jsx`, `json`, `bash`, `sh` or `shell`. Shown as a label on its own line above the code, at the end edge. Any other value is shown, not highlighted

### How it works
A `<pre>` with a `<code>` inside, styled by `components/code.css`. Highlighting is optional, from `highlight.js`.

- `highlightBlock(pre)` colours one block: it wraps the code in six `.tok-*` classes, one per `--luz-code-*` token.
- `initHighlight()` does it for every `pre.luz-code-block`, adds an `aria-label` to a block that has none ("CSS example"), and adds a copy button inside each block. Core gives that button no position: place it with your own CSS, or call `highlightBlock()` alone. `luz.js` runs `initHighlight()`.
- In forced colors every colour becomes the system text colour; bold keywords and italic comments stay.

### Without JavaScript
The block is plain, readable text in one colour. Nothing is lost but the colours.

### Keyboard and ARIA
A block can be wider than the screen, so it must take focus: Tab reaches it and the arrow keys scroll it.

- `tabindex="0"`, `role="region"` and an `aria-label` that names the code, so the focus stop has a name.
- Inline code needs nothing.

### When to use
Use a code block for code or terminal output the reader may read or copy, and inline code for names inside a sentence.

### When not to use
Do not use a code block for a long file or for text that is not code.

- For a whole file, link to the source.
- For a key the reader presses, use `<kbd>`.

### Do and don't
- **Do** Code that works when it is pasted: the command alone.
- **Don't** A prompt sign and the output in the same block: pasted, the “$” and the output lines fail.

### Writing the content
Show code that works when it is pasted.

- Name each block in its `aria-label`: what the code is, not "Code".
- Set `data-lang`; use `text` for output that is not code.
- Keep lines short: a long line makes the reader scroll sideways.

## Color mode switcher
URL: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/mode-switcher/
Example: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/examples/components/mode-switcher.html
Files: components/mode-switcher.css · Package: @luz-ds/core

Lets readers choose light, dark or high contrast: radios that work without JavaScript, or one button that cycles.

### Known issues
A stored color mode can flash once on load: `initThemeSystem()` is a deferred module and runs after the first paint, and LUZ ships no script for the `<head>`, by design. This site sets the mode before the first paint with a small script of its own.

### Copy the markup
Radio group markup
```html
<fieldset class="luz-mode-switcher">
  <legend class="luz-mode-switcher__label">Color mode</legend>
  <label class="luz-mode-btn" data-theme="light"><input class="luz-mode-btn__input" type="radio" name="luz-theme" value="light" checked>Light</label>
  <label class="luz-mode-btn" data-theme="dark"><input class="luz-mode-btn__input" type="radio" name="luz-theme" value="dark">Dark</label>
  <label class="luz-mode-btn" data-theme="high-contrast"><input class="luz-mode-btn__input" type="radio" name="luz-theme" value="high-contrast">High contrast</label>
</fieldset>
```

The cycle variant: the same radios, an icon in each label, and a button with one icon per mode.

Cycle variant markup
```html
<fieldset class="luz-mode-switcher luz-mode-switcher--cycle">
  <legend class="luz-mode-switcher__label">Color mode</legend>
  <button class="luz-mode-cycle" type="button" aria-label="Change color mode">
    <svg class="luz-mode-btn__icon" data-mode-icon="light" viewBox="0 0 24 24" aria-hidden="true">…</svg>
    <!-- the same for data-mode-icon="dark" and "high-contrast" -->
  </button>
  <span class="luz-mode-cycle__status" role="status"></span>
  <label class="luz-mode-btn" data-theme="light">
    <input class="luz-mode-btn__input" type="radio" name="luz-theme" value="light" checked>
    <svg class="luz-mode-btn__icon" viewBox="0 0 24 24" aria-hidden="true" focusable="false">…</svg>
    Light
  </label>
  <!-- the same for dark and high-contrast -->
</fieldset>
```

Mode script code
```js
import { initThemeSystem, initThemeCycle } from "@luz-ds/core/theme";
initThemeSystem();
initThemeCycle();
```

### Variants and options
- `.luz-mode-switcher`: The radio group, as a row of buttons; the checked one is filled
- `.luz-mode-switcher--cycle`: One button instead of the radios, when scripting is on
- `.luz-mode-cycle`: The cycle button; shows the icon whose `data-mode-icon` matches the checked radio
- `.luz-mode-cycle__status`: A hidden live region for the new mode; added by the script if missing
- `name="luz-theme"`: The radio name the tokens and `theme.js` listen to

### How it works
A native radio group, styled by `components/mode-switcher.css`. The radios are the control and the source of truth.

- The tokens re-scope the page from the checked radio with `:root:has()`, so choosing a mode works with no script.
- `initThemeSystem()` from `theme.js` sets `data-theme` on `<html>`, and stores the choice under `luz-theme` in `localStorage`. It starts from the attribute on `<html>`, light if there is none: [to start from the system's setting](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/tokens/modes/#system), set the attribute before it runs.
- `initThemeCycle()` turns each `--cycle` group into one button. Each press checks the next mode and fires its `change` event, so whatever listens to the radios applies it. It adds the button if the markup has none.
- A look of your own ([make one](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/tokens/themes/)) joins the choice when its name is listed in `data-luz-themes` on `<html>`: a stored value is accepted only for the three modes and for those names.
- `luz.js` runs both.
- To add an Auto choice that follows the system setting or the time of day, wrap the radios, with a fourth one for it, in [`<luz-mode>`](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/site/mode/) from `@luz-ds/site`.

### Without JavaScript
The three radios show, even in the cycle variant, and choosing one changes the mode of the page. The choice is not remembered on the next page.

### Keyboard and ARIA
Radios: Tab reaches the group, the arrow keys choose a mode.

- The cycle button: Tab reaches it, Enter or Space moves to the next mode.
- Its name says what it does and the current mode: "Change color mode. Current: Dark".
- A polite status announces the new mode: "Color mode: Dark".

### When to use
Offer a color mode switcher on every page of a site, in the same place, so readers can pick the mode they read best in.

- The radio group where there is room, such as a settings page or a sidebar footer.
- The cycle variant where space is short, such as a header or a page footer.

### When not to use
Do not use the cycle variant where readers compare the modes: the radio group shows all three at once.

- Do not hide it on a settings page only: a reader who cannot read the page cannot find the setting.

### Do and don't
- **Do** Name the modes for what they are: “Light”, “Dark”, “High contrast”.
- **Don't** “Accessible” for the high-contrast mode: it says the other modes are not, and does not say what changes.

### Writing the content
Call the group "Color mode" and the modes "Light", "Dark" and "High contrast".

- Each mode keeps its visible name next to its icon, so the radios read without the icons.

## Copy button
URL: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/copy-button/
Example: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/examples/components/copy-button.html
Files: components/copy-btn.css · Package: @luz-ds/core

Copies a command or a value to the clipboard, and says it did.

### Known issues
The Clipboard API needs a secure context (https, or localhost while you develop). Elsewhere the copy fails. The failure is announced to screen readers only: the button shows no message, so a sighted reader sees nothing happen. The text can still be selected and copied by hand.

### Copy the markup
Copy button markup
```html
<code class="luz-code-inline">npm install @luz-ds/core</code>
<button class="luz-copy-btn" type="button" data-copy="npm install @luz-ds/core" aria-label="Copy the install command">Copy</button>
```

Copy script code
```js
import { initCopyButtons } from "@luz-ds/core/clipboard";
initCopyButtons();
```

### Variants and options
One class and one attribute. The look does not change.

- `.luz-copy-btn`: Small mono button, 24 px high; hidden until the script runs
- `data-copy`: The exact text to copy
- `.is-copied`: Set by the script for about a second after a copy: success colour, label "Copied"

### How it works
A native `<button>`, styled by `components/copy-btn.css` and wired by `clipboard.js`.

- `initCopyButtons()` listens for clicks on any `.luz-copy-btn` and copies its `data-copy`. `luz.js` runs it.
- For about a second the label reads "Copied", then goes back.
- A polite live region says "Copied to clipboard", or that the copy failed. The texts come from `i18n.js`, in the language of the page.
- `copyToClipboard(text, el)` does the same for your own controls.

### Without JavaScript
The button is hidden, because it would do nothing. The text it copies stays on the page, so the reader selects and copies it.

### Keyboard and ARIA
Tab reaches the button; Enter or Space copies. Focus stays on the button.

- The visible label is "Copy"; the `aria-label` starts with it and says what is copied: "Copy the install command".
- The result is announced in a polite live region shared by every copy button.

### When to use
Use a copy button for a short string the reader will paste somewhere else: a command, a token name, a key.

### When not to use
Do not use a copy button where selecting the text is just as easy, or as the only way to get the content.

- For long text, show it in a [code block](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/code/) the reader can select.

### Do and don't
- **Do** Next to the text it copies, which the reader can also select by hand.
- **Don't** A copy button on text the reader must change first: they paste “<your-token>” and the command fails.

### Writing the content
Keep the visible label "Copy", and name what it copies in the accessible name.

- Start the accessible name with the visible word: "Copy the install command".
- Copy exactly what is shown, without a prompt sign or extra spaces.

## Dropdown
URL: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/dropdown/
Example: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/examples/components/dropdown.html
Files: components/dropdown.css · Package: @luz-ds/core

A button that opens a short list of actions or links, anchored under it.

### Known issues
There are no arrow keys: Tab moves between the actions, as in any list of buttons. A browser without CSS anchor positioning opens the list as a sheet at the bottom of the screen instead of under the button.

### Copy the markup
Dropdown markup
```html
<div class="luz-dropdown">
  <button class="luz-btn luz-btn--secondary" type="button" popovertarget="project-actions">Actions</button>
  <div class="luz-dropdown__menu" id="project-actions" popover>
    <ul class="luz-dropdown__list">
      <li><a class="luz-dropdown__item" href="/project/edit/">Edit</a></li>
      <li><button class="luz-dropdown__item" type="button">Duplicate</button></li>
      <li><hr class="luz-dropdown__separator"></li>
      <li><button class="luz-dropdown__item luz-dropdown__item--danger" type="button">Delete project</button></li>
    </ul>
  </div>
</div>
```

### Variants and options
- `.luz-dropdown`: The wrapper: the button and its panel, side by side in the source. It scopes the anchor, so several dropdowns on a page each open under their own button
- `popovertarget` and `popover`: The button names the panel by its `id`; the panel is the popover. The browser does the rest
- `.luz-dropdown__menu`: The panel: a surface with an edge and a shadow, at least 12 rem wide, scrolling when it is taller than 24 rem
- `.luz-dropdown__list`: The `<ul>` of actions
- `.luz-dropdown__item`: A link or a button, at least 44 px high and the width of the panel
- `.luz-dropdown__item--danger`: A destructive action, in the danger color
- `aria-disabled="true"`: An action that is not available now: disabled text color, and it keeps its place in the tab order so a reader can find out it exists
- `.luz-dropdown__separator`: A rule between two groups of actions, an `<hr>` in its own `<li>`

### How it works
A native [popover](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Popover_API) opened by a button with `popovertarget`, styled by `components/dropdown.css`. There is no JavaScript.

- The browser puts the panel in the top layer, closes it on Escape or a click outside, returns the focus to the button and tells assistive technology whether it is expanded.
- Where the browser has CSS anchor positioning (Chrome and Edge 125, Safari 26, Firefox 147) the panel opens under the button at its start edge, and flips above when there is no room. Without it the panel is a sheet at the bottom of the screen.
- In a browser without the popover API the list stays in the page, under the button, and every action still works.
- It is a list of actions, not an ARIA `menu`: that role promises arrow keys, a roving tabindex and typeahead, which LUZ does not script. Plain links and buttons keep every behaviour the browser gives them.

### Without JavaScript
Nothing changes: the popover is HTML. The actions that are buttons need your own script to do something, as any button does; the ones that are links work as they are.

### Keyboard and ARIA
Enter or Space on the button opens the panel; the focus stays on the button, and the panel follows it in the tab order. Tab moves to the first action, then through the others, and Shift+Tab goes back. Escape closes the panel and returns the focus to the button.

- Give the button a name that says what is inside: “Actions”, “More options for Ana”, not a bare “…”.
- An unavailable action uses `aria-disabled="true"` and no `disabled`, so it stays reachable and a screen reader says it exists. Do not run its action when it is activated.
- The panel is not a dialog and holds no form: for a decision or a form, use the [modal](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/modal/).

### When to use
Use a dropdown for three to seven related actions on one thing, when showing them all would crowd the page: the actions of a row in a table, of a card, of a project.

### When not to use
Do not use a dropdown to pick a value, or to hide the main action.

- To pick one value of a form, use a [select](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/select/).
- For the main action of a page, use a visible [button](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/button/).
- For the sections of a site, use a [sidebar](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/sidebar/) or a navigation list.
- LUZ has no context menu on right click. The browser's own menu is the reader's, and replacing it breaks copy, paste and spelling help; give the same actions in a dropdown.

### Do and don't
- **Do** Name the actions with verbs and put the destructive one last, apart.
- **Don't** Nouns that do not say what happens, and a dangerous action in the middle.

### Writing the content
Start each action with a verb, in the order a reader would look for it.

- Two or three words: “Duplicate”, “Move to archive”.
- Say what the destructive action destroys: “Delete project”, not “Delete”.
- Group with a separator, not with headings.

## Figure
URL: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/figure/
Example: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/examples/components/figure.html
Files: components/figure.css · Package: @luz-ds/core

Shows an image, a chart or a diagram with a caption that says what it is.

### Known issues
None known.

### Copy the markup
Figure markup
```html
<figure class="luz-figure">
  <div class="luz-figure__media">
    <img src="requests.png" width="640" height="192" alt="Bar chart: requests rise every day, from 1,200 on Monday to 3,400 on Saturday.">
  </div>
  <figcaption class="luz-figure__caption">Requests per day, last six days.</figcaption>
</figure>
```

### Variants and options
There are no modifiers.

- `.luz-figure`: A padded surface with a brand-coloured start border and rounded corners
- `.luz-figure__media`: Rounds and clips the image, chart or code inside
- `.luz-figure__caption`: Smaller, italic, secondary text colour

### How it works
The native `<figure>` and `<figcaption>`, styled by `components/figure.css`. No JavaScript.

- The caption names the figure for assistive technology.
- A bare `<figure>` with no class also gets a simple style from the base elements.

### Without JavaScript
Nothing changes: a figure is HTML and CSS.

### Keyboard and ARIA
A figure is not interactive and takes no focus.

- The media needs its own text alternative: `alt` on an `<img>`, or `role="img"` and `aria-label` on an inline `<svg>`.
- A chart also needs its numbers as text: in the alt text, the caption or a [table](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/table/) next to it.

### When to use
Use a figure for a chart, an image, a diagram or a code sample that the text refers to and that needs a caption.

### When not to use
Do not use a figure for decoration.

- A decorative image gets `alt=""` and no figure.
- For a picture in a box of fixed shape, use the [image](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/image/) frame.

### Do and don't
- **Do** A caption that says what the figure shows, and for what period.
- **Don't** “Figure 1” as the caption: the reader learns the number, not what the chart says.

### Writing the content
The caption says what the figure shows, and for what period or scope.

- The alt text says what the reader would see: the trend, not "chart".
- Do not repeat the caption in the alt text.

## Form fields
URL: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/form/
Example: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/examples/components/form.html
Files: components/form.css · Package: @luz-ds/core

Collect input with native fields, choices and pickers, each with a visible label, a hint and an error.

### Known issues
None known.

### Copy the markup
Text field with a hint markup
```html
<div class="luz-field">
  <label class="luz-field__label" for="project-name">Project name</label>
  <input class="luz-input" id="project-name" type="text" aria-describedby="project-name-hint">
  <div class="luz-field__helper" id="project-name-hint">Shown on the dashboard.</div>
</div>
```

Field with an error markup
```html
<div class="luz-field">
  <label class="luz-field__label" for="slug">Slug</label>
  <input class="luz-input luz-input--error" id="slug" type="text" aria-invalid="true" aria-describedby="slug-error">
  <div class="luz-field__error" id="slug-error"><span class="u-sr-only">Error: </span>Use letters, numbers and dashes only.</div>
</div>
```

Radio group markup
```html
<fieldset class="luz-fieldset">
  <legend>Plan</legend>
  <div class="luz-check-group">
    <div class="luz-check-item"><input type="radio" name="plan" id="plan-free" checked><label for="plan-free">Free</label></div>
    <div class="luz-check-item"><input type="radio" name="plan" id="plan-team"><label for="plan-team">Team</label></div>
  </div>
</fieldset>
```

Switch markup
```html
<label class="luz-toggle">
  <input class="luz-toggle__input" type="checkbox" role="switch">
  <span class="luz-toggle__track" aria-hidden="true"><span class="luz-toggle__thumb"></span></span>
  <span class="luz-toggle__label">Weekly digest</span>
</label>
```

### Variants and options
Every control is a native element with a LUZ class. The state comes from native attributes.

- `.luz-field`: Wraps one label, its control, its hint and its error
- `.luz-field__label`: The visible label
- `.luz-field__label--required`: Adds a red " *" after the label
- `.luz-field__helper`: A hint under the control
- `.luz-field__error`: An error under the control, in the danger colour
- `.luz-input`: Text, email, number, date, time, colour, file and range inputs and `<textarea>`; 44 px high
- `.luz-input--error`: A 2 px danger underline; pair it with `aria-invalid="true"`
- `.luz-input--textarea`: Auto height, at least 80 px, resizes vertically
- `.luz-select`: A `<select>`, on its own page: [Select](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/select/)
- `.luz-check-group`, `.luz-check-item`: A list of checkboxes or radios, each with its label
- `.luz-fieldset`: A bordered group with an upper-case `<legend>`
- `.luz-toggle`: A switch: a checkbox with `role="switch"` drawn as a track and a thumb
- `.luz-meter`: A `<meter>` bar, in the brand colour in every state: see [Meter](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/meter/)
- `.luz-output`: A computed value
- `disabled`, `readonly`: Faded; read-only also gets a dashed underline

### How it works
Native form controls, styled by `components/form.css`. No JavaScript: the browser owns the state, the keyboard, validation and submission.

- Each control gets its name from its `<label>`; the hint and the error are tied to it with `aria-describedby`.
- LUZ does not mark a field as invalid for you: add `.luz-input--error`, `aria-invalid="true"` and the error text when your validation fails.
- Field text is 16 px at 768 px and below and on touch screens, so iOS Safari does not zoom in.

### Without JavaScript
Every control works and submits with its form, including the switch. Only what your own script adds is missing, such as live validation or a value echoed in an `<output>`.
