```html
<luz-timeline role="group" layout="vertical" aria-label="Versions of the library">
  <ol class="luz-timeline">
    <li class="luz-timeline__item">
      <time class="luz-timeline__date" datetime="2024-02">February 2024</time>
      <h3 class="luz-timeline__title">Version 0.1</h3>
      <p class="luz-timeline__text">Buttons, forms and tables.</p>
    </li>
    <li class="luz-timeline__item">
      <time class="luz-timeline__date" datetime="2024-09">September 2024</time>
      <h3 class="luz-timeline__title">Version 0.2</h3>
      <p class="luz-timeline__text">Dark mode and a print stylesheet.</p>
    </li>
    <li class="luz-timeline__item">
      <time class="luz-timeline__date" datetime="2025-05">May 2025</time>
      <h3 class="luz-timeline__title">Version 0.3</h3>
      <p class="luz-timeline__text">Right-to-left layouts.</p>
    </li>
  </ol>
</luz-timeline>
```

For a timeline added to the page after it has loaded, import the module once. It defines the element, and there is no `init` to call:

Timeline script code
```js
import "@luz-ds/core/timeline";
```

### Variants and options
The options are attributes of `<luz-timeline>`. Each item has a date, a title and a text.

- `aria-label`: The name of the timeline. Write it with `role="group"`: a name on an element without a role is not read. If you leave the role out, the script adds it
- `layout="vertical"`: Every item stays visible down a line. The item in the middle of the screen is active, the ones before it are past
- `autoplay`: Opts in to moving on by itself, with a visible Pause and Play button. Horizontal only; off unless you write it
- `interval`: Milliseconds between items with `autoplay`. The default is 5000; a value under 2000 is raised to 2000
- `data-luz-label-previous`, `-next`, `-pause`, `-play`: The names of the buttons, when LUZ does not ship the language of the page or you want other words
- `--luz-timeline-paper`: The colour behind the timeline, which the hump on the rail and the empty dots are painted with. The default is `--luz-surface-page`; on a card, set it on the element to the card's surface: `style="--luz-timeline-paper: var(--luz-surface)"`
- `.luz-timeline__date`: A `<time>`. Its text is the label of the date button on the rail, so give each item a different one. Without it the button shows the item's number
- `.luz-timeline__title`: A `<p>`, or a heading of the level your page needs: the class stays the same
- `.luz-timeline__text`: One or two sentences; a link is allowed
- `data-luz-state`: Written by the script on the items of a vertical timeline: `active` or `past`. Do not set it yourself

### How it works
A custom element around a native ordered list, with styles from `components/timeline.css` and a script, `timeline.js`. `luz.js` loads the script only on a page that has a `<luz-timeline>`. The element looks for the first `.luz-timeline` inside it; with none, it does nothing.

- **Horizontal.** The script builds, with DOM methods only, Previous and Next at the sides of the card and a rail of dates under it: one button per item, with the text of its date. The cards share one grid cell, so the band is as tall as the longest card and nothing jumps when you change the item. The cards that are not current are `inert` and hidden. In the current card the date is hidden from sight, because the rail shows it.
- **Changing the item.** Click a date, use Previous and Next, the arrow keys, Home and End on the rail, or swipe more than 40 px sideways with a finger or the mouse. Toward the start of the line is the next item. Past either end it wraps round. A swipe that ends on a link is not a click on it.
- **The rail.** The current date is scrolled to the middle, with a smooth scroll only if the visitor has not asked for reduced motion. A keyboard move keeps the focus on the new current date, and so does a change that hides the card the focus was in.
- **Vertical.** The script marks the item crossing the middle of the screen `data-luz-state="active"` and the ones before it `past`. The line behind a past item takes the brand colour, and the active dot is filled and larger. It runs with reduced motion too, without the transition.
- **Autoplay.** With `autoplay`, the item changes every `interval` milliseconds, in a loop. The Pause button under the rail stops it; it then reads Play and starts it again. The timeline also waits, without a change to the button, while the pointer moves over it (it goes on after 4 seconds still, or when the pointer leaves), while the keyboard focus is inside it, while less than half of it is on screen and while the tab is hidden. With reduced motion it never starts and the button is not shown.
- **Text.** "Previous", "Next", "Pause" and "Play" are in the language of the page when LUZ ships it (English, Spanish), chosen by the nearest `lang`, or yours through `registerLocale()` and `data-luz-label-*`. They travel with the script, so `@luz-ds/core/timeline` works on its own. With `luz.js` on the page, a language you add with `registerLocale()` reaches them too. See [the JavaScript modules](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/get-started/javascript/).

### Without JavaScript
An ordered list, with every item visible: a line down the inline-start side with a dot at each item, then the date, the title and the text. The list looks the same before the script has defined the element, so nothing jumps when it does. Autoplay, the rail, Previous and Next, the swipe and the active mark of the vertical layout need JavaScript.

### Keyboard and ARIA
Tab reaches, in this order: Previous, the links in the current card, Next, the current date on the rail and the Pause or Play button. The other dates are not in the Tab order: the arrow keys move between them.

- **Left and Right** on the rail move to the previous and the next date, and the focus goes with them. In right-to-left text they swap. Past either end it wraps.
- **Home and End** go to the first and the last date.
- **Enter or Space** on a date, Previous, Next or Pause presses it: they are native buttons.
- The element has `role="group"` and your `aria-label`. The current date has `aria-current="true"`; only that date is tabbable (a roving `tabindex`).
- The cards are one live region. It is `aria-live="polite"` when the visitor changes the item, and `off` while autoplay runs, so a card that changes by itself is not announced.
- The Pause or Play button's name is its action. The arrows' names are "Previous" and "Next": see the known issues.
- The cards that are not current are `inert`: they take no focus and are not read. If the focus was in the card that goes, it moves to the new current date.
- Each card has `aria-posinset` and `aria-setsize`, so a screen reader can say "2 of 4" when only one card is shown.

### When to use
Use a timeline for a short run of events with dates, where the order is the point: releases, milestones, a company's history.

- Horizontal, when each event needs a card and the reader goes through them one by one.
- Vertical, when the reader should see every event as they scroll.
- Four to ten items. Beyond that the rail needs a lot of scrolling.

### When not to use
Do not use a timeline for steps the reader has to follow in order, or for events without dates.

- For a process, use a numbered list.
- To compare events across attributes, use a [table](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/table/).
- When the reader needs to see every item at once, use the vertical layout: the horizontal one shows a single card.
- Do not turn on autoplay for content the reader must not miss. Nobody has to wait for the next card.

### Do and don't
- **Do** A title that says what happened, with the date in one format.
- **Don't** A vague title and dates in different formats: the reader has to open the card to learn what happened, and cannot compare the dates.
- **Do** A `<time>` with a different text in each item: it is the name of the button on the rail.
- **Don't** Leave out the date: the rail then has buttons named "1" and "2", and the reader cannot tell them apart.

### Writing the content
Put the date first, then what happened, in few words.

- The date: the same format in every item, and a different text in each. It is the name of a button.
- The title: two to five words, sentence case, no full stop. Say the event: "Public launch", not "News".
- The text: one sentence, a few lines at most. In the horizontal layout the band is as tall as the longest card, so keep the cards about the same length.
- Use the `datetime` attribute so the date can be read by machines, such as `2025-06`.

## Toast
URL: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/toast/
Example: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/examples/components/toast.html
Files: components/toast.css · Package: @luz-ds/core

Confirms a small result, such as "Draft saved", without interrupting the reader.

### Known issues
LUZ ships the look only. The live region, the placement, the timing and the close button's behaviour are yours to build, and to make accessible.

### Copy the markup
Keep an empty live region on the page, and put the toast inside it when the result happens.

Toast in its live region markup
```html
<div role="status">
  <div class="luz-toast">
    <div class="luz-toast__content">
      <div class="luz-toast__kind">Saved</div>
      <div class="luz-toast__msg">Draft saved.</div>
    </div>
    <button class="luz-toast__close" type="button" aria-label="Dismiss notification">×</button>
  </div>
</div>
```

### Variants and options
There are no modifiers.

- `.luz-toast`: A raised box on the strong surface, 320 px wide at most and never wider than its container
- `.luz-toast__kind`: A small mono label above the message
- `.luz-toast__msg`: The message
- `.luz-toast__close`: The × button, 28 px at least

### How it works
A styled block from `components/toast.css`. LUZ has no toast script.

- Position it with your own CSS, for example fixed at the bottom of the screen, above the page with `--luz-z-toast`.
- If it hides by itself, leave it on screen for at least 5 seconds and keep it while it has focus or the pointer is over it.
- The close button needs your script to remove the toast.

### Without JavaScript
A toast only appears in answer to something your script did, so it does not exist without JavaScript. Show the same result on the page, for example in an [alert](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/alert/) after a form is sent.

### Keyboard and ARIA
Showing a toast does not move focus.

- Insert it into a polite live region (`role="status"`) that is already on the page, so screen readers announce it.
- The close button is reachable with Tab, and named "Dismiss notification".

### When to use
Use a toast to confirm a small result that needs no answer: "Draft saved", "Link copied".

### When not to use
Do not use a toast for anything the reader must act on or must not miss: it goes away.

- For an error, use an [alert](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/alert/) next to what failed.
- For a decision, use a [modal](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/modal/).
- Do not put links or buttons in it, other than the close button.

### Do and don't
- **Do** A short confirmation the reader can miss without harm: “File exported.”
- **Don't** A failed payment in a toast: it goes away before the reader acts. Use an alert next to what failed.

### Writing the content
One short line, in the past tense: "File exported."

- The kind label is one word: "Saved", "Success".
- Do not repeat what the page already shows.

## Tooltip
URL: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/tooltip/
Example: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/examples/components/tooltip.html
Files: components/tooltip.css · Package: @luz-ds/core

Adds a short hint to a control on hover or focus; never essential content.

### Known issues
Partly fails WCAG 1.4.13 (content on hover or focus): Escape does not close the tooltip, so the reader has to move the pointer or the focus away. Keep tooltips short and non-essential. Listed in the [accessibility statement](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/accessibility/).

### Copy the markup
Tooltip markup
```html
<div class="luz-tooltip">
  <button class="luz-btn luz-btn--outline" type="button" aria-describedby="archive-tip">Archive</button>
  <div class="luz-tooltip__text" role="tooltip" id="archive-tip">Hides the project from the list</div>
</div>
```

### Variants and options
One position: above the control, centred. Where the browser has CSS anchor positioning, the tip moves below the control when there is no room above. There are no modifiers.

- `.luz-tooltip`: Wraps the control and the tip, and opens the tip on hover and on focus inside
- `.luz-tooltip__text`: The tip: one line, on the strong surface, with a shadow

### How it works
CSS only, from `components/tooltip.css`: the tip shows while the wrapper is hovered or holds focus.

- It stays open while the pointer moves from the control onto the tip.
- It fades in and out over `--luz-duration-fast`, and appears at once under reduced motion.
- The tip does not wrap: keep it short, or it can overflow a narrow screen.
- **Enhancement:** in browsers with CSS anchor positioning (Chrome and Edge 125, Safari 26, Firefox 147: Newly available, not yet Widely available), the tip is anchored to its own control (`anchor-scope` and `anchor()` insets) and flips below it when there is no room above. Outside a size container it is no longer clipped by an ancestor that hides overflow; inside one, such as a table wrapper or a player, it is placed and clipped by that box, as before. In other browsers it stays above, as before: the rules sit inside `@supports`, with no script.

### Without JavaScript
Nothing changes: the tooltip has no script.

### Keyboard and ARIA
Focus the control with Tab and the tip shows; move the focus away and it hides.

- `aria-describedby` on the control points at the tip, so screen readers read it after the control's name.
- The tip has `role="tooltip"` and never takes focus.
- The control keeps its own name: the tip is a description, not a label.

### When to use
Use a tooltip to add a short explanation to a control whose label is clear but brief.

### When not to use
Do not put anything essential, long or interactive in a tooltip.

- Touch screens have no hover: put information people need on the page, as a hint ([form fields](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/form/)).
- Never use a tooltip as the only name of an icon button.
- No links or buttons inside it.

### Do and don't
- **Do** A short phrase that adds something to the label: what “Archive” does.
- **Don't** A tooltip that repeats the label: “Save” then “Saves the project” makes the reader wait for nothing.

### Writing the content
One short phrase that says what the control does or why: "Hides the project from the list".

- Do not repeat the control's label.
- No full stop on a fragment.

## Layout objects
URL: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/layout/
Files: objects/_objects.css · Package: @luz-ds/core

Lay out blocks in a stack, a row, a grid or beside an image, a group of actions, and the page itself with its sticky bar, with the o-* classes.

### Examples

`.o-shell`, `.o-main` and `.o-container` are page-level: [this page uses them](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/layout/#page-nav).

### Pick an object

Objects only lay things out: no colour, no type. Spacing comes from the space tokens.

- `.o-stack`: A column, 12 px between items
- `.o-row`: A row that wraps, items centred vertically, 12 px between them
- `.o-grid`: A grid with 16 px gaps; set the columns with your own `grid-template-columns`, or with one of the modifiers below
- `.o-grid--auto`: As many equal columns as fit, none narrower than `--luz-grid-min` (16 rem by default): the grid reflows by itself and needs no breakpoint
- `.o-grid--2`, `.o-grid--3`, `.o-grid--4`: That many equal columns above 768 px; one column at 768 px and below
- `.o-grid--split`: Two equal columns when each gets `--luz-grid-min` (16 rem by default), one below: a hero with its image, or two features side by side. It stacks by itself with larger text
- `.o-media`, `.o-media__body`: A fixed item, such as an avatar, beside content that takes the remaining width
- `.o-container`: The content width (`--luz-content-max`, 1100 px) and page padding; less padding at 640 px and below
- `.o-container--inline`: The container's width and side gutters only, with no padding above or below: the row of a bar, so its content starts where the page's content starts
- `.o-page`: A page without a sidebar: a column at least as tall as the window, whose `<main>` grows, so the footer rests on the bottom of a short page. Any number of bands can come before the header
- `.o-sticky`: A bar that stays at the top while the page scrolls, in a window at least 30 rem tall, with the scroll padding that keeps what Tab reaches out from under it
- `.o-actions`: Two or three related buttons or links in a row that wraps, 8 px apart; at 640 px and below, a column of full-width actions whose labels wrap
- `.o-shell`: The app layout: a sidebar column (`--luz-sidebar-width`) beside the main area, a footer across the bottom; one column at 768 px and below
- `.o-main`: The main area inside `.o-shell`

### The page and its bars

A page without a sidebar is `.o-page`: any bands first (a notice, the cookie question), then the header, `<main>` and the footer. The header's row is `.o-container.o-container--inline`, so the site's name starts where the content starts, and `.o-sticky` keeps the header at the top.

Page markup
```html
<body>
  <a class="luz-skip-link" href="#main-content">Skip to main content</a>
  <div class="o-page">
    <header class="o-sticky">
      <div class="o-container o-container--inline o-row">…</div>
    </header>
    <main id="main-content" class="o-container o-stack" tabindex="-1">…</main>
    <footer>
      <div class="o-container o-container--inline o-row">…</div>
    </footer>
  </div>
</body>
```

- The objects lay out only: the header's surface and divider are the job of your CSS, or of the header of a package for one kind of site.
- `--luz-bar-h` is the height of a one-row bar of 44 px controls at the default text size: the control, two 4 px paddings and a 1 px divider. The [navbar](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/navbar/) panel opens at that height when nothing anchors it.
- With `.o-sticky` on the page, the scroll padding of `<html>` is `--luz-bar-h` or 3.5em, whichever is more, plus half a control: a field reached with Tab, or the target of the [skip link](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/skip-link/), stops below the bar. It is a minimum: a bar that wraps to several rows with enlarged text is taller, and Safari can leave a field partly under it at 300 percent text.
- Below 30 rem of window height the bar scrolls away with the page, so it never takes most of a short screen.

### Actions and the split grid

Split grid and actions markup
```html
<section class="o-grid o-grid--split">
  <div class="o-stack">
    <h1>…</h1>
    <div class="o-actions">
      <a class="luz-btn luz-btn--primary" href="/register/">Register now</a>
      <a class="luz-btn luz-btn--outline" href="/programme/">See the programme</a>
    </div>
  </div>
  <div class="luz-image">…</div>
</section>

<!-- two columns only when each gets 24 rem -->
<section class="o-grid o-grid--split hero">…</section>
<style>.hero { --luz-grid-min: 24rem; }</style>
```

- One primary action per group, and a second, outline one if there is another way. In the narrow column the primary comes first, as in the source.
- A `.luz-btn` in `.o-actions` wraps its label in the narrow column, so a long label never runs out of the window.

### The grid

LUZ has no 12-column system: a content grid is a handful of equal columns, and `.o-grid` draws them. Use `.o-grid--auto` when the items decide how many fit, such as cards; use `.o-grid--2` to `--4` when the number is part of the design.

Grid markup
```html
<!-- as many columns as fit, each at least 16 rem -->
<div class="o-grid o-grid--auto">…cards…</div>

<!-- at least 12 rem: set the property in your own CSS -->
<div class="o-grid o-grid--auto gallery">…</div>
<style>.gallery { --luz-grid-min: 12rem; }</style>

<!-- three columns above 768 px, one below -->
<div class="o-grid o-grid--3">…</div>
```

- Items keep their source order: the grid reorders nothing, so reading order and tab order are the page's.
- Columns are `minmax(0, 1fr)`, so a long word or a wide table inside an item cannot push the grid wider than its container.
- For a layout that depends on the width of a card and not of the window, put the grid in a container and size the items there; the objects do not read the container.

### Lists

When the items are a list (posts, speakers, tags), put `.o-grid`, `.o-stack` or `.o-row` on the `<ul>` or `<ol>` itself. The object takes off the markers and the indent, and the items stay a list: a screen reader says how many there are and lets the reader skip past them.

List grid markup
```html
<ul class="o-grid o-grid--auto">
  <li class="luz-card">…</li>
  <li class="luz-card">…</li>
</ul>
```

- Safari can drop the list role from a list without markers, outside a `<nav>`. Give each item a heading, as cards have, so the reader can still move through them.
- No rule of yours is needed. Inside [prose](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/prose/), which gives lists their markers back, a list with an object keeps none.

### Copy the markup

Media object markup
```html
<div class="o-media">
  <span class="luz-avatar luz-avatar--md" aria-hidden="true">AB</span>
  <div class="o-media__body">
    <p>Ana Belén</p>
  </div>
</div>
```

App shell markup
```html
<body class="o-shell">
  <nav class="luz-sidebar" aria-label="Main">…</nav>
  <main class="o-main" id="main-content">
    <div class="o-container">…</div>
  </main>
  <footer>…</footer>
</body>
```

The footer is a plain `<footer>`, which core places across the bottom: nothing here needs site. For whole pages without a sidebar, use [`.o-page`](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/layout/#objects-page). [What each package needs](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/get-started/structure/#needs) lists every piece.

## Utility classes
URL: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/utilities/
Files: utilities/_utilities.css · Package: @luz-ds/core

Small u-* classes that do one thing each, for the cases a component does not cover.

Use a utility for a one-off adjustment. If you add the same utilities to the same element again and again, you need a component or a class of your own.

- Utilities win over components: they come last in the cascade.
- `.u-sr-only` hides text from the screen but not from screen readers. `.u-hidden` hides it from both.
- `.u-no-events` only stops the pointer: a keyboard can still reach and use the element. Never use it to disable a control.

**All 16 utility classes**

## Keyframes
URL: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/keyframes/
Files: components/_animations.css · Package: @luz-ds/core

Five shared animations for your own components, which stop when the reader asks for reduced motion.

A fifth keyframe, `luz-fade-in`, opens the modal.

### Use a keyframe

Name the keyframe in your own `animation`, and take its duration from a [motion token](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/tokens/motion/).

Panel that slides in code
```css
.panel[open] {
  animation: luz-slide-up var(--luz-duration-base) var(--luz-easing-enter);
}
```

- Under reduced motion every `--luz-duration-*` token is `0s`, so the animation does not run and the element shows in its final state.
- A hard-coded duration ignores reduced motion: never write one.
- Do not loop an animation for ever: stop it when the task ends.

- `luz-spin`: One full turn, for a loading indicator
- `luz-shimmer`: Moves a background gradient across, for a loading placeholder
- `luz-pulse`: Grows and fades out, then back, to draw the eye once
- `luz-slide-up`: Fades in while rising 8 px, for something that appears
- `luz-fade-in`: Fades in, used by the modal and its backdrop

## Site
URL: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/site/

Six self-contained components that need data of the site: search, cookie consent, color mode, language switch, submenu and banner, and how to tell whether you need them.

Level 3 · @luz-ds/site

Six self-contained components that need data of the site: search, cookie consent, color mode, language switch, submenu and banner, and how to tell whether you need them.

A piece is here when it needs data of the site: its search index, its cookie policy, its languages, its menu, an announcement. Each is a `<luz-*>` tag that works on its own, in any header or page. Everything else is a **component** of core, one reusable piece that fits inside anything; components are in [Components](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/).

The page structure (the header, the hero, the footer, the page header) is in the packages for one kind of site: [landing](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/landing/) for a landing page and [CMS](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/cms/) for a blog, a newspaper or any CMS. They work without this package, and take its components where a search or a language switch goes.

- Each tag is the block, and its parts are `.luz-<tag>__<part>`; every rule uses semantic tokens only.
- [The LUZ home page](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/) and these docs are built with them.
- Not sure which package a piece belongs to? [What each package needs](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/get-started/structure/#needs) lists every piece, with the package it is in.

### Use site when

- You want a site search, a cookie banner or a language switch without writing them yourself.
- Your header has a few links grouped under one button.
- You need a short announcement above the header on every page.

### Use core alone when

- You only need components such as buttons, forms and cards.
- Your site has no search, no optional cookies and one language.
- You build a single widget, not a whole page.

### Your own components on top

Style what you add with semantic tokens too, so it follows the color mode and any [theme of your own](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/tokens/themes/).

Semantic tokens in an app-level component
```css
.my-panel {
  background: var(--luz-surface);
  border: 1px solid var(--luz-divider);
  color: var(--luz-text-primary);
}

.my-panel:hover {
  background: var(--luz-surface-muted);
  border-color: var(--luz-outline);
}

/* Not a primitive colour: it would stay the same in dark mode */
/* color: var(--luz-gray-100); */
```

## Submenu
URL: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/site/submenu/
Example: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/examples/site/submenu.html
Files: <luz-submenu> · Package: @luz-ds/site

Groups a few links of a header under one button, so the header keeps a short row of links.

### Known issues
A submenu is a native `<details>`, which has no Escape key and does not close when you click elsewhere: it closes when you press its button again or open another one (in browsers that support `name` on `<details>`: Chrome and Edge 120, Safari 17.2, Firefox 130; in older ones several can be open at once). From 769 px an open box stays over the top of the page until then, and if you keep pressing Tab after it, a link of the page behind it can be hidden (WCAG 2.2 success criterion 2.4.11, Focus not obscured). In the menu at 768 px and below this does not happen: the links are in the flow and Escape closes the whole menu. It has not been tested with a screen reader.

### Copy the markup
An item of the list of core’s [navbar](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/navbar/), in a [landing](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/landing/header/) or [CMS](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/cms/header/) header, whose content is a `<luz-submenu>` around a `<details>`: its `<summary>` is the button, and a list of links follows it. No class: the tag is the block, and its parts are found by their place. Give every submenu of the header the same `name`, so opening one closes the others.

Submenu markup
```html
<nav class="luz-navbar" id="site-nav" aria-label="Main" popover>
  <ul class="luz-navbar__list">
    <li><a class="luz-navbar__link" href="/" aria-current="page">Home</a></li>
    <li>
      <luz-submenu>
        <details name="site-menu">
          <summary>Wines</summary>
          <ul>
            <li><a class="luz-navbar__link" href="/wines/red/">Red wines</a></li>
            <li><a class="luz-navbar__link" href="/wines/white/">White wines</a></li>
          </ul>
        </details>
      </luz-submenu>
    </li>
    <li><a class="luz-navbar__link" href="/visits/">Visits</a></li>
  </ul>
</nav>
```

### Variants and options
There are no variants. The attributes are the browser’s.

- `<luz-submenu>`: Around the `<details>`, with `display: contents`: it draws no box and adds no role. The `<summary>` looks like the links beside it, with a chevron; the list of links is indented under it, and from 769 px a box under it
- `name`: The same value on every submenu of the header: opening one closes the others. Browsers without it leave the others open
- `open`: Set by the browser. Do not write it in the markup: a submenu open on every page hides the page under it

### How it works
CSS from `@luz-ds/site` and a native `<details>`. No JavaScript: `<luz-submenu>` is a tag that no script ever defines.

- The browser opens and closes it, and tells assistive technology whether it is open. A submenu opens on a click, a tap, Enter or Space: never on hover, so it does not open under a pointer passing by, and it works the same on a touch screen.
- At 768 px and below, inside the header’s menu, the links of a group open in place, under their button, indented, and push the next links down.
- From 769 px, where the header’s links are a row, they open in a box under their button, over the page; the page does not move. The box of the last item opens toward the start of the row, so it stays in the window, in either direction of text.
- The chevron is drawn with two borders and has no text: the state is the one the browser exposes.
- It does not use the popover API: a popover sits in the top layer, so it could not open in place inside the menu.

### Without JavaScript
Nothing changes: there is no script. The links are plain links.

### Keyboard and ARIA
- **Order:** a closed submenu is one stop, its button. Open, its links come right after it, then the next item of the header.
- **Keys:** Enter or Space on the button opens and closes it; focus stays on the button. Tab and Shift+Tab move through the links. Escape does nothing in a submenu (see Known issues); in the header’s menu at 768 px and below it closes the menu and returns focus to the menu button.
- **Names:** the button’s name is its text. The browser exposes the expanded state of a `<summary>`: write no `aria-expanded`, no `role="menu"` and no `role="menuitem"`; these are links in a navigation landmark, not an application menu.
- **Current page:** put `aria-current="page"` on the link of the page, in the submenu too.

### When to use
Use it when the header needs more links than fit in a short row, and some of them belong together: the kinds of wine, the pages about the company.

### When not to use
Do not use it for a single link, or to hide pages most visitors need: put those in the row itself.

- Do not nest a submenu in a submenu: two levels hide pages from the visitor and are hard to use with a pointer and a keyboard.
- Do not put actions, forms or settings in it: it holds links to pages. For actions use buttons, or a [dropdown](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/dropdown/).
- If every group has many links, give each group a page of its own and link to it: a long submenu is a page in a box.

It replaces a dropdown navigation built with a script, and the hover menu. Nothing in LUZ is removed.

### Do and don't
- **Do** Name the group with a word that tells the visitor what is in it, and keep it to a handful of links.
- **Don't** Use a vague group name such as “Resources” or “More”: the visitor has to open it to know whether what they want is there.

### Writing the content
Name the group with one or two words in sentence case that say what it holds: “Wines”, “About us”.

- Name each link after the page it opens, so it makes sense outside the group: “Red wines”, not “Red”.
- Do not make the group’s name a page of its own as well: the button opens the group, it does not go anywhere. If the group has an overview page, make it the first link: “All wines”.
- Keep the same groups, in the same order, on every page.

## Banner
URL: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/site/banner/
Example: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/examples/site/banner.html
Files: <luz-banner>, tone="warning" · Package: @luz-ds/site

Tells every visitor one short thing at the top of the page, such as a sale, an event or planned maintenance.

### Known issues
It cannot be closed: a close button needs a script, and a choice that lasts from page to page needs storage. Keep the banner short and remove it from the markup when it ends. In a browser without CSS anchor positioning (before Chrome and Edge 125, Safari 26, Firefox 147), the header’s menu at 768 px and below opens at the top of the window, so before the page scrolls it covers part of the header under a banner; Escape or a click outside closes it.

### Copy the markup
A `<luz-banner>` around one `<section>` named by its first words, after the [skip link](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/skip-link/) and the [cookie consent](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/site/consent/), before the header of the page (a [landing](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/landing/header/) or [CMS](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/cms/header/) header).

Banner markup
```html
<a class="luz-skip-link" href="#main">Skip to main content</a>
<luz-banner>
  <section aria-labelledby="banner-label">
    <p><strong id="banner-label">Open day.</strong> Visit the winery on Saturday 25 October,
      from 11:00 to 18:00. <a href="/visits/">Book a visit</a></p>
  </section>
</luz-banner>
<header>…</header>
```

### Variants and options
- `<luz-banner>`: Around one `<section>`, which becomes a band as wide as its container, on a muted surface with a rule under it, in small sans text. Its text starts where the header’s row starts. A tag that no script defines: no class, no role of its own
- `tone="warning"`: On the tag, the one tone: The warning colours: for something that stops the visitor doing what they came to do, such as maintenance. Say it in the words too: “Planned maintenance.” Any other value leaves the plain band

### How it works
CSS from `@luz-ds/site`. No JavaScript: `<luz-banner>` is a tag that no script ever defines.

- It is a band of the page, in the flow: it scrolls away with the page, and an `.o-sticky` header stays at the top under it. Nothing covers the page.
- Its inline padding lines its text up with the header’s row, up to `--luz-content-max` wide, in either direction of text.
- There is no close button. Closing it for good needs a script and a value stored in the browser, and a button that does nothing without a script is never shown. A banner is short-lived: remove it from the markup when the event is over.
- There is no success or error tone: a banner is not the answer to something the visitor did. For that use an [alert](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/alert/) in the page.

### Without JavaScript
Nothing changes: there is no script.

### Keyboard and ARIA
- **Order:** its link comes after the skip link and before the header.
- **Landmark:** a `<section>` with a name is a region, so a screen reader lists it among the landmarks; name it with `aria-labelledby` pointing at its first words. If it says nothing more than its sentence, a `<div>` with no name is fine.
- **Not a live region:** it is there when the page loads, so it needs no `role="status"` or `role="alert"`; a screen reader reads it with the rest of the page.

### When to use
Use it for one short, timely thing every visitor of the site should know, on every page, for a few days: a sale, an event, planned maintenance, a change of opening hours.

### When not to use
Do not use it for something that belongs to one page or to one visitor: put that in the page, or answer with an [alert](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/alert/) or a [toast](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/toast/).

- Do not show two banners at once, and do not leave one up for months: a band that never changes is no longer read.
- Do not use it to ask for cookies: use the [cookie consent](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/site/consent/) banner.
- Do not put a form or more than one link in it.

It replaces the announcement bars a site builds with its own CSS. Nothing in LUZ is removed.

### Do and don't
- **Do** Start with what it is about, in bold, say when, and end with one link that says where it goes.
- **Don't** Rely on the yellow to say it is a warning, shout in capitals, or leave out the date: the words alone must carry the message, and “soon” is wrong a day later.

### Writing the content
One sentence, two at most. Start with what it is about, in bold, ending with a full stop: “Open day.”, “Planned maintenance.”.

- Give the date and the time, with the day of the week, so it is still true when read late.
- End with one link that says where it goes: “Book a visit”, not “More information”.
- Write in sentence case, with no exclamation marks.

## Cookie consent
URL: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/site/consent/
Example: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/examples/site/consent.html
Files: .luz-consent, __title, __choices · Package: @luz-ds/site

Asks a visitor once whether the site may use optional cookies, with Accept and Reject side by side, and remembers the answer.

### Known issues
Without JavaScript the banner is not shown at all: there is nothing to answer, because none of the site’s own scripts run either. A server that sets optional cookies itself, without a script, must ask some other way. The answer is kept in the browser’s local storage, so a server cannot read it, and clearing site data asks again. In a window less than 30 rem (480 px) tall the banner is not fixed: it is in the flow at the top of the page, where its markup is, so the page moves down when it appears. The saved state hides when focus leaves it for the page, but not when you click an empty part of the page: use its Close button. It has not been tested with a screen reader.

### Copy the markup
Right after the [skip link](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/skip-link/), before a [banner](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/site/banner/) and the header of the page (a [landing](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/landing/header/) or [CMS](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/cms/header/) header): it shows at the bottom of the window, but it comes first in the reading and Tab order. One checkbox per category of optional cookies, its `value` the category’s name. `site.min.js` loads the banner’s own file, `consent.min.js`, when the browser is idle; a page without `site.min.js` loads that file on its own.

Cookie consent markup
```html
<script type="module" src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@luz-ds/site@0.1.0/dist/site.min.js"></script>

<a class="luz-skip-link" href="#main">Skip to main content</a>
<luz-consent>
  <section class="luz-consent" data-luz-consent aria-labelledby="consent-title" hidden>
    <div data-luz-consent-ask>
      <h2 class="luz-consent__title" id="consent-title">Cookies on Bodega Albar</h2>
      <p>We use cookies that this site needs to work. We would also like to measure how you
        use it, to improve it. <a href="/cookies/">Read the cookie policy</a>.</p>
      <form class="o-actions">
        <button class="luz-btn luz-btn--primary" type="submit" value="all">Accept optional cookies</button>
        <button class="luz-btn luz-btn--primary" type="submit" value="none">Reject optional cookies</button>
      </form>
      <details class="luz-consent__choices">
        <summary>Choose which cookies to allow</summary>
        <form class="o-stack">
          <fieldset class="luz-fieldset">
            <legend>Optional cookies</legend>
            <div class="luz-check-group">
              <label class="luz-check-item"><input type="checkbox" value="analytics"> Measuring visits</label>
              <label class="luz-check-item"><input type="checkbox" value="marketing"> Adverts on other sites</label>
            </div>
          </fieldset>
          <div class="o-actions">
            <button class="luz-btn luz-btn--secondary" type="submit">Save my choices</button>
          </div>
        </form>
      </details>
    </div>
    <div data-luz-consent-done tabindex="-1" hidden>
      <p>Your choice is saved. You can change it at any time on the
        <a href="/cookies/">cookie policy</a> page.</p>
      <button class="luz-btn luz-btn--secondary" type="button" data-luz-consent-close>Close</button>
    </div>
  </section>
</luz-consent>
<header>…</header>

<!-- On the cookie policy page -->
<button class="luz-btn luz-btn--outline" type="button" data-luz-consent-open hidden>Change cookie settings</button>
```

Your scripts read the answer and listen for a new one. Load an optional script only for a category the visitor granted:

Script that reads the answer
```js
import { getConsent } from "@luz-ds/site/consent";

const granted = (answer) => answer?.granted.includes("analytics");

if (granted(getConsent())) startMeasuring();
document.addEventListener("luz:consent", (event) => {
  if (granted(event.detail)) startMeasuring();
  // Withdrawn: the simplest correct answer is to reload the page
  else location.reload();
});
```

### Variants and options
There are no variants. The hooks are `data-luz-consent-*` attributes.

- `.luz-consent`: The banner: a band fixed at the bottom of the window, as wide as it, at most half its height and scrolling inside, its text in the header’s column, in the sans. In a window less than 30 rem tall it is in the flow instead. Keep `hidden` on it: the script shows it
- `.luz-consent__title`: Its heading, in the sans; it names the banner’s region through `aria-labelledby`
- `.luz-consent__choices`: The `<details>` with the categories, under the two buttons
- `<luz-consent>`: The custom element the module defines. It wires the banner inside it when it connects
- `data-luz-consent`: On the `<section>`: the banner. Optional `data-luz-consent-days`, how long an answer lasts (180 days by default, 395 at most), and `data-luz-consent-key`, the storage key (it must start with `luz-`)
- `data-luz-consent-ask`, `data-luz-consent-done`: The question, and the confirmation that takes its place. The confirmation has `tabindex="-1"`: it takes focus
- `data-luz-consent-close`: On a button inside the confirmation: hides the banner and returns focus to the button that opened it, or the first `data-luz-consent-open` button, or `<main>`. The confirmation also hides when focus leaves it for the page
- `value="all"`, `value="none"`: On the submit buttons: Accept grants every category, Reject none. A submit button with another value, or none, grants the ticked ones of its form
- `data-luz-consent-open`: On a button anywhere, with `hidden`: its space is kept, the script shows it, and it shows the banner again, with the stored answer ticked
- `--luz-consent-h`: Set on `:root` by the script while the banner shows: its height. The page, `.o-main` and `.luz-sidebar` keep that much room at their end, and scroll what Tab reaches above the banner

### How it works
CSS from `@luz-ds/site`, two native forms and a file of its own, `@luz-ds/site/consent` (`dist/consent.min.js`, under 1 kB compressed), which defines `<luz-consent>`. `site.min.js` loads it when the browser is idle, and only on a page with a `<luz-consent>`, so no other page pays for it. A banner added after the page has loaded needs the file imported by hand; two copies of it on one page define the element once.

- **When it asks:** when no answer is stored, when the stored one has expired, or when the banner offers a category the stored answer was not asked about. Then it shows, as a band at the bottom of the window, so nothing on the page moves: it traps nothing and takes no focus, and the page keeps room for it at its end and scrolls what Tab reaches above it, so the page can be read and used before answering.
- **The answer:** Accept grants every category, Reject none, Save my choices the ones ticked. Enter in a checkbox saves the ticked ones, never all. Escape is not an answer: nothing happens. The confirmation then takes the place of the question and takes focus, and is read. It goes away with its Close button, or when focus leaves the banner for the page; focus stays where it went.
- **Where it is kept:** in the browser’s `localStorage`, under `luz-consent`, as JSON: `{"version":1,"expires":…,"asked":["analytics","marketing"],"granted":["analytics"]}`, with `expires` in milliseconds since 1970. Not in a cookie: a cookie would travel to the server with every request, and asking about cookies should not need one. No personal data, and nothing leaves the browser. A malformed value counts as no answer. If storage is blocked, the answer holds for the page and the next page asks again.
- **Your scripts:** `getConsent()` returns the stored answer, `{ asked, granted, expires }`, or `null`. Each new answer dispatches `luz:consent` on `document`, with the same object as `detail`. Category names are a lowercase letter, then lowercase letters, digits or hyphens, 32 at most.
- **Changing the answer:** as easy as giving it. A button with `data-luz-consent-open`, on the cookie policy page, shows the banner again. Put one banner on a page: every such button opens it.
- The script writes no text: every word is in your markup, in the page’s language.

### Without JavaScript
The banner and the button that shows it again stay hidden, by their `hidden` attribute. Without a script none of the site’s own scripts run, so there is nothing to ask about, and buttons that would do nothing are never shown. Link the cookie policy from the footer of every page, so it can always be read.

### Keyboard and ARIA
- **Order:** the skip link stays first, so a returning visitor can still jump to the content. The banner comes next, before the header, although it shows at the bottom: the policy link, Accept, Reject, then the button that opens the categories.
- **Keys:** Enter or Space on a button; Space ticks a checkbox. Escape does nothing: it does not hide the banner.
- **Landmark:** a `<section>` named by its heading is a region, listed among the landmarks, before the banner landmark of the header. It is not a dialog: it does not block the page, so it needs no `role="dialog"`.
- **Focus:** none when the page loads. After an answer, the confirmation; after the button that shows it again, the banner. Close returns it to that button, or to the first such button, or to `<main>`; never to the top of the page.

### When to use
Use it when your site sets cookies, or stores data in the browser, that it does not need to work, such as measuring visits or adverts: the law in the EU and the UK asks for the visitor’s consent before that.

### When not to use
Do not use it when the site sets only the cookies it needs to work (a session, a basket, a language or colour choice): those need no consent. Say so in the cookie policy and show no banner.

- Do not use it as a wall that hides or blocks the page until the visitor answers.
- Do not use it for news or a sale: that is a [banner](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/site/banner/).

It replaces a third-party consent script. Nothing in LUZ is removed.

### Do and don't
- **Do** Give Accept and Reject the same style, side by side, with words that say what each one does.
- **Don't** Make Accept a big button and hide Reject in a small link or behind settings: an answer pushed one way is not free consent.

### Writing the content
Say in a sentence what the site needs and what it would like, and why, in plain words. Name the heading after the site: “Cookies on Bodega Albar”.

- Write the buttons as the action and the thing: “Accept optional cookies”, “Reject optional cookies”; never “OK”, “Got it” or “Agree”.
- Name each category after what it does for whom: “Measuring visits”, “Adverts on other sites”, not “Performance” or “Targeting”.
- Link the cookie policy by its name, and say in the confirmation where the answer can be changed.

## Auto color mode
URL: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/site/mode/
Example: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/examples/site/mode.html
Files: <luz-mode>, remember, by="clock" · Package: @luz-ds/site

Adds an Auto choice to the color mode switcher, so the page follows the system setting or the time of day until the reader chooses a mode.

### Known issues
What to expect:

- With `by="clock"`, Auto is dark from 20:30 to 07:30 even when the device is set to light. The system setting is not read.
- With `prefers-contrast: more` and a dark setting together, Auto gives the high-contrast mode, which is light.
- In the Auto state the cycle button says Auto, not the mode Auto applied.
- Without [the script for the head](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/site/mode/#boot), a dark system can flash the wrong mode first.
- Auto and the legend are yours to translate. A name in `data-luz-themes` is left to core.
- It has not been tested with a screen reader.

### Copy the markup
Core's [color mode switcher](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/mode-switcher/) with a fourth radio, `auto`, checked, inside `<luz-mode>`. `site.min.js` loads the element's file, `mode.min.js`; a page without it loads that file on its own.

Put the icons in the labels, not `data-mode-icon` on the cycle button: with `luz.js` the button copies the checked label's icon, and core has no Auto icon for `data-mode-icon`.

Auto color mode markup
```html
<script type="module" src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@luz-ds/site@0.1.0/dist/site.min.js"></script>

<luz-mode remember by="clock">
  <fieldset class="luz-mode-switcher luz-mode-switcher--cycle">
    <legend class="luz-mode-switcher__label">Color mode</legend>
    <label class="luz-mode-btn"><input class="luz-mode-btn__input" type="radio" name="luz-theme" value="auto" checked><svg class="luz-mode-btn__icon" viewBox="0 0 24 24" aria-hidden="true"><circle cx="12" cy="12" r="9" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><path d="m8 16 4-8 4 8m-6-3h4" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/></svg>Auto</label>
    <label class="luz-mode-btn" data-theme="light"><input class="luz-mode-btn__input" type="radio" name="luz-theme" value="light"><svg class="luz-mode-btn__icon" viewBox="0 0 24 24" aria-hidden="true"><circle cx="12" cy="12" r="5" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="12" cy="12" r="8.6" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2.4" stroke-dasharray="1.5 4.8"/></svg>Light</label>
    <label class="luz-mode-btn" data-theme="dark"><input class="luz-mode-btn__input" type="radio" name="luz-theme" value="dark"><svg class="luz-mode-btn__icon" viewBox="0 0 24 24" aria-hidden="true"><path fill="currentColor" d="M20.5 14.5A8.5 8.5 0 0 1 9.5 3.5a8.5 8.5 0 1 0 11 11Z"/></svg>Dark</label>
    <label class="luz-mode-btn" data-theme="high-contrast"><input class="luz-mode-btn__input" type="radio" name="luz-theme" value="high-contrast"><svg class="luz-mode-btn__icon" viewBox="0 0 24 24" aria-hidden="true"><circle cx="12" cy="12" r="9" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><path fill="currentColor" d="M12 3a9 9 0 0 1 0 18Z"/></svg>High contrast</label>
  </fieldset>
</luz-mode>
```

#### Script for the head

This script, for `by="system"`, avoids the flash of the wrong mode: it sets `data-theme` before the first paint. It is recommended, not required. It takes the mode stored under `luz-theme`, then `prefers-contrast`, then `prefers-color-scheme`.

Under a CSP without `'unsafe-inline'`, serve it as a classic file in the `<head>` or allow it by its `'sha256-…'` hash.

Script for the head
```html
<script>
  (function () {
    var m;
    try { m = localStorage.getItem("luz-theme"); } catch (e) {}
    if (["light", "dark", "high-contrast"].indexOf(m) < 0)
      m = matchMedia("(prefers-contrast: more)").matches ? "high-contrast"
        : matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches ? "dark" : "light";
    document.documentElement.dataset.theme = m;
  })();
</script>
```

### Variants and options
There are no variants. The attributes of `<luz-mode>`:

- `remember`: A boolean. Stores the choice under `luz-theme`, core's key. Auto removes it. Without it a reload starts in Auto
- `by`: What Auto follows: `system` (the default) or `clock`
- `for`: The `id` of the element that gets the attributes. `<html>` by default
- `light-attr`: The attribute that holds the phase of the day, `data-light` by default. Never `data-theme` or a `data-luz-*` attribute: they are not checked, and are the mode's and core's

### How it works
CSS from `@luz-ds/site` for the element's box and `@luz-ds/site/mode`, which defines `<luz-mode>`. `site.min.js` loads it when idle, on a page with a `<luz-mode>`. The radios and labels are core's: the element writes no text.

- **Auto by the system:** `prefers-contrast: more` gives `high-contrast`; otherwise `prefers-color-scheme: dark` gives `dark`; otherwise `light`. It follows a change while the page is open.
- **Auto by the clock:** `prefers-contrast: more` still wins. Otherwise the phase of the day decides: `dark` in the dark phases, `light` in the others, and it is written as `data-light`. It checks every minute and when the tab shows again.
- **A mode the reader chose:** It sets `data-theme` to it. With `by="clock"` the light is pinned: `afternoon` for Light, `night` for the others.
- **Storage:** only with `remember`, under core's `luz-theme`; a value that is not a mode is ignored.
- **With luz.js:** core's script ignores Auto, and its cycle button steps through all four.

The phases of the day, by the visitor's clock. Night runs through midnight.

- `night`: 22:30: 05:00: dark
- `dawn`: 05:00: 07:30: dark
- `morning`: 07:30: 12:00: light
- `afternoon`: 12:00: 17:30: light
- `sunset`: 17:30: 20:30: light
- `dusk`: 20:30: 22:30: dark

#### Properties, methods and event

- `el.mode`: The choice: `auto`, `light`, `dark` or `high-contrast`. Setting it chooses the radio
- `el.light`: The phase of the day now, or `null` unless `by="clock"`
- `preview(x)`: Shows another time of day: `x` is a phase name or an hour from 0 to 24. With Auto, `data-theme` follows it; with a mode chosen, only the light does. `preview(null)` goes back. Unless `by="clock"` it returns `false`
- `luz-mode:change`: Bubbles from the element at every change. Its `detail`: `mode` (the choice), `theme` (the `data-theme` applied), `light` (the phase, or `null`), `remembered` (`true` only with `remember` and a mode stored now) and `simulated` (`true` while a preview is active)

#### Two lights in one mode

With `by="clock"` the rest is your CSS: set only the semantic tokens that differ, as [a theme of your own](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/tokens/themes/) does. Measure each pair with the [contrast check](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/tokens/contrast/).

A day look and a night look
```css
[data-theme="light"][data-light="morning"] {
  --luz-surface-page: #fdf3dc;
  --luz-surface-muted: #fdf3dc;
  --luz-surface: #fffaf0;
}

[data-theme="dark"][data-light="night"] {
  --luz-surface-page: #0f1520;
  --luz-surface-muted: #0f1520;
  --luz-surface: #172030;
}
```

### Without JavaScript
The four radios show, even in the cycle variant, and core's tokens change the mode from the checked one. Auto is light. The system and the clock are not followed, and nothing is remembered.

### Keyboard and ARIA
- **Radios:** Tab reaches the group, the arrow keys choose Auto, Light, Dark or High contrast. With `luz.js`, the cycle button moves to the next of the four with Enter or Space.
- The legend and the labels are yours. The element adds no button, role or ARIA: the group is the fieldset and its radios.

### When to use
Use it when readers should not have to choose: the page follows their device or the time of day until they do.

- `by="system"` for a site that reads best in the light or the dark the reader's device is in.
- `by="clock"` for a site with a look for each part of the day, such as a venue or a weather page.

### When not to use
Do not use it when the site has one look in one mode: a switcher with no Auto is core's.

- Do not use `by="clock"` to promise the real sunrise: the hours are fixed.

### Do and don't
- **Do** Call the choice “Auto” and keep the other names as they are: the reader sees the four ways to choose at once.
- **Don't** Name it “Smart” or “Magic”: it does not say what the page follows, and a reader cannot tell it from a mode.

### Writing the content
Call the group “Color mode” and the choices “Auto”, “Light”, “Dark” and “High contrast”.

- Say near the switcher what Auto follows: “Auto follows your device” or “Auto follows the time of day”.

## Language switch
URL: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/site/lang-switch/
Example: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/examples/site/lang-switch.html
Files: <luz-lang-switch>, .luz-lang-switch, __button, __menu, __link · Package: @luz-ds/site

Lets readers go to the same page in another language, from a button in the header.

### Known issues
The list opens at a fixed place under the header, not under its button: placing it next to the button needs CSS anchor positioning, which is not yet available in every browser. Below 360 px wide the button shows the globe only, to keep the header on one row; the language’s name is still its accessible name, so a sighted reader has to recognise the globe. It has not been tested with a screen reader yet.

### Copy the markup
One link per language, to the same page in that language, in the header of every translated page. On each page mark its own language with `aria-current="page"` and write the label in the page’s language.

Language switch markup
```html
<luz-lang-switch>
  <button class="luz-lang-switch__button" type="button" popovertarget="lang-menu">
    <span class="u-sr-only">Language: </span><span class="luz-lang-switch__name">English</span>
  </button>
  <nav class="luz-lang-switch__menu" id="lang-menu" popover aria-labelledby="lang-title">
    <p class="luz-lang-switch__title" id="lang-title">Language</p>
    <ul class="luz-lang-switch__list">
      <li><a class="luz-lang-switch__link" href="/" hreflang="en" lang="en" aria-current="page">English</a></li>
      <li><a class="luz-lang-switch__link" href="/es/" hreflang="es" lang="es">Español</a></li>
      <li><a class="luz-lang-switch__link" href="/ar/" hreflang="ar" lang="ar">العربية</a></li>
    </ul>
  </nav>
</luz-lang-switch>
```

### Variants and options
There are no variants. One custom property places the list.

- `<luz-lang-switch>`: The block: holds the button and the list. A tag that no script defines, with no class and no role of its own
- `.luz-lang-switch__button`: A 44 px button with the current language’s name; filled while the list is open
- `.luz-lang-switch__icon`: An optional globe before the name, drawn in the text colour. Decorative: `aria-hidden="true"`
- `.luz-lang-switch__name`: The current language’s name. Below 360 px it is clipped and the globe shows alone; it stays in the button’s name
- `.luz-lang-switch__menu`: The popover: fixed under the header, at the end of the row (the left edge in right-to-left text)
- `.luz-lang-switch__title`: The visible name of the list
- `.luz-lang-switch__list`: The list of languages, without bullets
- `.luz-lang-switch__link`: One 44 px row per language. With `aria-current`: bold and underlined
- `--luz-lang-switch-top`: How far from the top of the screen the list opens. Defaults to `--luz-bar-h`, the height of a one-row bar of 44 px controls; set it on the tag if your header is taller.

### How it works
Changing language is going to another page, so the switch is a list of links. The button opens it with the native `popovertarget`, and `@luz-ds/site` only styles it: there is no script. `<luz-lang-switch>` is a tag that no script ever defines; it only gives the block a name in the markup and in CSS, and adds no role: the button and the `nav` carry the meaning.

- Each language is named in that language, with `lang` so a screen reader pronounces it, and `hreflang` so the link says where it goes.
- The list is a popover in the top layer, fixed under the header at the inline end; it mirrors in right-to-left text.
- The page itself declares its language and direction: `<html lang="ar" dir="rtl">`. Add a `<link rel="alternate" hreflang="…">` per language in the `<head>`, so search engines find the others.
- Core switches Arabic text to the system sans and removes letter spacing from it: the serif has no Arabic letters, and spacing breaks the joins of the script.

### Without JavaScript
Nothing changes: the button opens the list with the popover API, and the links are links. In a browser without the popover API the button is hidden and the links show in a row.

### Keyboard and ARIA
Tab to the button and press Enter or Space to open the list; Tab moves through the languages and Enter follows one. Escape, or a click outside, closes the list.

- The browser tells assistive technology whether the list is open, from `popovertarget`.
- The button’s name is “Language: English”: what it is, then the visible text (WCAG 2.5.3). Below 360 px only the globe shows, and the name is the same.
- The current language is a link with `aria-current="page"`.

### When to use
Use it on a site whose pages exist in two languages or more, in the header of every translated page, at the same place on each.

### When not to use
Do not add it to pages that exist in one language only, even if the rest of the site is translated.

- Do not choose the language for the reader from the browser’s settings or their location: let them choose, and link each page to the others.
- Do not use it to translate the page in place with a script: each language is a page of its own, with its own address.

It replaces nothing in LUZ. It makes a `<select>` with a script that changes the address unnecessary.

### Do and don't
- **Do** Name each language in that language, so a reader who does not understand the page still finds theirs.
- **Don't** Use flags, or name the languages in the page’s language: a flag is a country, not a language, and “Árabe” means nothing to a reader of Arabic.

### Writing the content
Write each language’s name as its speakers write it: “English”, “Español”, “العربية”, never “EN” or a flag.

- Write the label in the page’s language: “Language”, “Idioma”, “اللغة”.
- List the languages in the same order on every page.
- If some pages are not translated, link to the closest page that is, and say in its language that the rest is in another one.

## Search
URL: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/site/search/
Example: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/examples/site/search.html
Files: <luz-search>, .luz-search · Package: @luz-ds/site

Finds a page, a section or an HTML element of a site by name, from a button in the header.

### Known issues
The search has not been tested with a screen reader yet. Ctrl+K opens this search instead of the browser’s own web search box: use the address bar to search the web. With `site.js`, a Ctrl+K pressed before the search’s script has loaded loads it, then opens the dialog, after a short wait on a slow connection. At 400 percent zoom the whole dialog scrolls, so the field can move out of view while you read the results.

### Copy the markup
One `<luz-search>` holds the link to your index, the button that replaces it, and the dialog. Put it where the search goes, usually at the end of the header: the link and the button share one place, so nothing moves when the button takes over, and the closed dialog takes no space. Every text is yours: write it in the page’s language.

Search markup
```html
<luz-search>
  <a class="luz-search__fallback" href="/a-z/" data-luz-search-fallback>
    <svg class="luz-search__trigger-icon" viewBox="0 0 24 24" aria-hidden="true" focusable="false"><circle cx="11" cy="11" r="7"/><path d="m20 20-4-4"/></svg>
    <span class="luz-search__fallback-label">A–Z index</span>
  </a>
  <button class="luz-search__trigger luz-search__trigger--compact" type="button" data-luz-search-open
          aria-haspopup="dialog" aria-keyshortcuts="Control+K Meta+K" hidden>
    <svg class="luz-search__trigger-icon" viewBox="0 0 24 24" aria-hidden="true" focusable="false"><circle cx="11" cy="11" r="7"/><path d="m20 20-4-4"/></svg>
    <span class="luz-search__trigger-label">Search docs…</span>
    <kbd class="luz-search__trigger-key" aria-hidden="true">Ctrl K</kbd>
  </button>
  <dialog class="luz-modal luz-search" aria-labelledby="search-title"
          data-luz-search-src="/search-index.json"
          data-luz-label-results="{n} results"
          data-luz-label-result="1 result"
          data-luz-label-capped="{shown} of {n} results. Type more to narrow."
          data-luz-label-none="No results for “{query}”. Check the spelling or try a shorter word."
          data-luz-label-loading="Loading the search index…"
          data-luz-label-error="Search is not available right now.">
    <search class="luz-search__body">
      <div class="luz-search__head">
        <h2 class="luz-search__title" id="search-title"><label for="search-q">Search the documentation</label></h2>
        <form method="dialog"><button class="luz-btn luz-btn--ghost luz-search__close" aria-label="Close search">
          <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" aria-hidden="true" focusable="false"><path d="M6 6l12 12M18 6 6 18"/></svg>
        </button></form>
      </div>
      <div class="luz-search__field">
        <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" aria-hidden="true" focusable="false"><circle cx="11" cy="11" r="7"/><path d="m20 20-4-4"/></svg>
        <input class="luz-input" id="search-q" type="text" maxlength="100" autocomplete="off"
               spellcheck="false" enterkeyhint="go" autofocus aria-describedby="search-hint">
      </div>
      <p class="luz-field__helper" id="search-hint">Results update as you type. Arrow keys move through them.</p>
      <p class="luz-search__status" role="status"></p>
      <div class="luz-search__results" data-luz-search-results>
        <div hidden><h3>Pages</h3><ul data-luz-search-list="pages"></ul></div>
        <div hidden><h3>Sections</h3><ul data-luz-search-list="sections"></ul></div>
        <div hidden><h3>HTML elements</h3><ul data-luz-search-list="elements"></ul></div>
      </div>
      <p class="luz-search__foot">Can’t find it? <a href="/a-z/">Browse the A–Z index</a></p>
    </search>
  </dialog>
</luz-search>

<script type="module" src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@luz-ds/site@0.1.0/dist/site.min.js"></script>
```

### Variants and options
Every option is markup: a class or an attribute.

- `.luz-search__trigger--compact`: at 768 pixels and below, the trigger shows the magnifier only, 44 by 44 pixels, and so does the link next to it; their names stay their words, clipped, not removed. Give both an `<svg class="luz-search__trigger-icon">`.
- More than one trigger: every `[data-luz-search-open]` on the page opens the dialog, inside the element or not (this site has one in the header and one on the documentation home). One outside stays hidden until the search works, and takes no space until then: put it where its arrival moves nothing, such as the end of a section.
- An element with `data-luz-search-show="idle"` inside `[data-luz-search-results]` shows while the field is empty, for example a short list of popular pages; one with `data-luz-search-show="none"` shows when nothing matches.
- Leave out a `[data-luz-search-list]` to leave out that group.
- The texts the script writes are the `data-luz-label-*` attributes of the dialog: `results`, `result`, `capped`, `none`, `loading` and `error`, with `{n}`, `{shown}` and `{query}` in them. `data-luz-label-idle` is the text the status shows while the field is empty, for example “Type to search the documentation”. A missing label writes nothing.

### How it works
Load `site.min.js`, as a module. It loads nothing on a page without a `<luz-search>`. On a page with one, it loads the search’s own file, `search.min.js`, the first time the reader points at it or moves the focus into it, presses `Ctrl` + `K`, or when the browser is idle, whichever comes first. That file defines `<luz-search>`, a custom element in the light DOM (no Shadow DOM), and every one on the page wires itself.

- The button takes the link’s place, in the same space, so nothing moves. If the link has the keyboard focus or a pressed pointer at that moment, the swap waits until the reader leaves it, follows it or lets go: the focus is never moved.
- The button opens the native `<dialog>` with `showModal()`: the browser keeps the focus inside, closes it with Escape and returns the focus.
- The first time the dialog opens, the script reads the index.
- If `search.min.js` cannot load, the page stays as it is without JavaScript: the link works and the button stays hidden.
- A `<luz-search>` added after the page has loaded, by a router or a framework, is not seen by `site.min.js`: import `@luz-ds/site/search` (or `search.min.js`) yourself, and it wires itself when it connects. Two copies of the file on one page define the element once.

The index is a JSON file, version 1. Each list holds `[text, url, meta, lang]`; `meta` (shown muted after the text) and `lang` are optional, and URLs are relative to the file:

Search index format
```json
{
  "version": 1,
  "pages": [["Button", "components/button/", "Components"]],
  "sections": [["When to use", "components/button/#when", "Button › Design"]],
  "elements": [["<table> element, Tables", "html/tables/#el-table"]]
}
```

A result matches when its text and meta together contain every word typed, without regard to case or accents; the ones that start with the words come first. Each group shows 8 results at most, and the status line says how many there are.

What the component accepts, so that an index built from a CMS cannot harm the page:

- The JSON comes only from the page’s own origin, over http or https, and a redirect fails the request. Your Content-Security-Policy needs `connect-src 'self'`; to use an index from another site, host a copy on yours. The browser caches it like any file.
- Links are only `http:` and `https:` URLs; any other item is left out. Text is written as text, never as HTML.
- Limits: 1,000,000 characters of JSON, 10,000 results, 300 characters a text, 8 words a search, 100 characters in the field. Unknown fields are ignored. An index that is not version 1 shows the error text.

### Without JavaScript
The button stays hidden, takes no focus and is not read, and the link shows in its place: write a page that lists every page by name, such as an A–Z index. The dialog is never opened.

### Keyboard and ARIA
Everything works from the keyboard, with one shortcut.

- `Ctrl` + `K` or `⌘` + `K` opens the search from anywhere on the page, except while typing in a text area or an editable region, or while another dialog is open. Pressed again, it selects the text in the field. Pressed before `search.min.js` has loaded, it loads it and then opens the dialog; on a page without a `<luz-search>` the browser keeps the key.
- Down arrow moves from the field to the first result; Down and Up move between results, across groups; Home and End go to the first and last. Up on the first result goes back to the field.
- Enter in the field opens the first result; on a result it follows the link. Typing on a result goes back to the field.
- Escape or the close button (an × icon named *Close search* by its `aria-label`) closes the dialog, whatever the field holds, and the focus returns to where it was. The field is `type="text"` for that reason: in a `type="search"` field, Chrome and Safari use the first Escape to clear the text. A result on the same page closes it and moves the focus to that section’s heading. If nothing had the focus when it opened (Ctrl+K on a page just loaded, or a click in a browser that does not focus buttons), the script moves it to the button that opened the dialog, or to the search’s own button after Ctrl+K, so the next Tab continues from the header.
- The heading names the dialog and labels the field. The count is announced once the reader stops typing (`role="status"`). Results are links in lists under headings, not a combobox.

### When to use
Use search on a site of more than a few pages, where readers look for something by its name: a component, a setting, an article title.

### When not to use
Do not use search instead of navigation: keep the menu and an index page.

- Search needs typing, and a name the reader may not know.
- It matches titles and headings only: it cannot search inside long texts or across many sites.

### Do and don't
- **Do** Say what is searched, in a short label that fits every language.
- **Don't** The magnifier alone on a wide screen: the reader has to guess what it searches, and the shortcut hint is gone. Keep the icon-only trigger for narrow screens.

### Writing the content
Every text is in the markup, so it is yours to write, in the page's language.

- The trigger says what is searched: “Search docs…”. Keep it short in every language (“Buscar…”) rather than cutting it off.
- Give section results their page in the meta: “When to use” with “Button › Design”, so a result makes sense on its own and is found by the page’s name.
- Say what to try next in the `none` label, which the status line announces: “Check the spelling or try a shorter word.” after the query.
- Point the fallback link and the line under the results at the same index page.

## Class reference
URL: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/site/classes/
Files: components/search.css, components/consent.css, components/lang-switch.css, components/submenu.css, components/banner.css · Package: @luz-ds/site

Every tag and class of the site components, what element it goes on and what it does, in one place.

Look up a tag or a class by name. Each component's own page has its markup and guidance. The page structure that site held before, from the shell to the footer, is in core ([layout](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/layout/), [skip link](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/skip-link/), [image](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/image/), [band](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/band/)) and in the packages for one kind of site ([landing](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/landing/), [CMS](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/cms/)).

### Search

- <luz-search>: <luz-search>: The element `search.min.js` defines. It holds the fallback link, the trigger and the dialog; the link and the trigger share one place, so nothing moves when the trigger takes over.
- .luz-search__fallback: <a>: The link to an index of every page, shown until the search works. A control high, with the magnifier before its words.
- .luz-search__fallback-label: <span>: The link’s words, also its name. Clipped, not removed, next to a compact trigger at 768 pixels and below.
- .luz-search__trigger: <button>: The search button, shaped like a field: label, then the shortcut. Hidden in the markup, in its place; the script shows it.
- .luz-search__trigger--compact: <button>: Modifier. At 768 pixels and below, the magnifier only, and the link next to it too; the words stay their names.
- .luz-search__trigger-icon: <svg>: The magnifier, in the text color, in the trigger and the link.
- .luz-search__trigger-label: <span>: The visible label, which is also the button’s name.
- .luz-search__trigger-key: <kbd aria-hidden="true">: The shortcut hint, "Ctrl K". Hidden on touch screens and from assistive technology, which reads `aria-keyshortcuts`.
- .luz-search: <dialog>: With `.luz-modal`: the search dialog, a column whose results scroll; full screen at 768 pixels and below.
- .luz-search__body: <search>: The field, the status and the results.
- .luz-search__head: <div>: The title and the close button, in one row that wraps.
- .luz-search__title: <h2>: The dialog’s name; its label names the field.
- .luz-search__field: <div>: The field, with a decorative magnifier `svg` at its start.
- .luz-search__status: <p>: The count of results, `role="status"`, small and muted.
- .luz-search__close: <button>: The close button, 44 pixels high, in a `form method="dialog"`.
- .luz-search__results: <div>: The result groups: a heading and a list of links each.
- .luz-search__foot: <p>: The last line, with the link to the index page.

### Language switch

- <luz-lang-switch>: a tag: The block: holds the button and the list, with no class and no role of its own. Sets `--luz-lang-switch-top`, how far down the list opens (core’s `--luz-bar-h` by default).
- .luz-lang-switch__button: <button>: Opens the list with `popovertarget`. Shows the current language; its name starts with the label, hidden.
- .luz-lang-switch__icon: <svg>: The globe, decorative, in the text color.
- .luz-lang-switch__name: <span>: The current language’s name in the button. Clipped below 360 pixels, where the globe shows alone; it stays in the button’s name.
- .luz-lang-switch__menu: <nav>: The popover with the list, fixed under the header at the end of the row.
- .luz-lang-switch__title: <p>: The visible name of the list, which labels the nav.
- .luz-lang-switch__list: <ul>: The languages, one per row, without bullets.
- .luz-lang-switch__link: <a>: A language, named in itself, with `lang` and `hreflang`; bold and underlined with `aria-current`.

### Submenu

- <luz-submenu>: around a <details>: A tag, no class: an item of a header’s links that holds more links. The `<summary>` is the button, the `<ul>` after it the links. No script.

### Banner and cookie consent

- <luz-banner>: around a <section>: A tag, no class: a band above the header with one short announcement and one link, its text in the header’s column. No script, no close button.
- tone="warning": <luz-banner>: The warning colours, for something that stops the visitor; the words say it too.
- .luz-consent: <section hidden>: The cookie banner, in a `<luz-consent>` before the header, shown as a band fixed at the bottom of the window. Hidden in the markup: `consent.min.js` shows it when no answer is stored.
- .luz-consent__title: <h2>: The banner’s heading, in the sans; it names the region.
- .luz-consent__choices: <details>: The categories of optional cookies, as checkboxes in a form, under Accept and Reject.

## Landing
URL: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/landing/

What a landing page needs on top of core, from its header and hero to the blocks of an event page, and how to tell whether you need it.

For one kind of site · @luz-ds/landing

What a landing page needs on top of core, from its header and hero to the blocks of an event page, and how to tell whether you need it.

A landing page is one page that presents a product or an event and asks the visitor to act. This package holds the patterns only that kind of page uses. The page column, the sticky bar, the skip link and the header’s links are core’s; the search, the cookie banner and the language switch are [Site](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/site/)’s, and optional.
