- Every class starts with `.luz-landing-`, uses semantic tokens only and sits in the cascade layer `luz.landing`, after site's.
- It has no script. Load `landing.css` after the CSS of tokens, core and site: [Install LUZ](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/get-started/#site-kinds) has the command and the CDN tags.
- It has a version of its own, 0.x while it grows, and needs version `^0.1.0` of tokens, core and site, declared as peer dependencies.
- [The LUZ home page](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/) is built with it.

### Use landing when

- You build the page of a product, a service or an event, with features to show side by side.
- You want blocks to copy for such a page: hero, programme, speakers, tickets, call to action and registration.

### Use site alone when

- Your pages are articles, documentation or an app: a header, the content and a footer.
- You lay out your own blocks with core's grid objects.

## Header
URL: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/landing/header/
Example: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/examples/landing/header.html
Files: .luz-landing-header, __brand, __actions · Package: @luz-ds/landing

Starts every page of a landing site with its name, its main links and a few controls, in one row that stays at the top.

### Known issues
The header's own issues are those of the pieces of core it is made of.

- **The menu panel.** If you keep pressing Tab after the last link of the open menu, focus moves on into the page and the menu stays open over it; Escape closes it. Without CSS anchor positioning the panel and the language list open at the height of a one-row header from the top of the window, so with enlarged text they can cover part of the header. See the [navbar's known issues](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/navbar/#known-issues).
- **Sticky header and enlarged text.** The scroll padding of `.o-sticky` is a minimum: at 300% text, with the header wrapped to several rows, Safari can leave a field reached with Tab under it. Set `scroll-padding-block-start` on `html` to your header's real height, or leave out `.o-sticky`.

### Copy the markup
Header markup
```html
<header class="luz-landing-header o-sticky">
  <div class="o-container o-container--inline o-row">
    <button class="luz-nav-toggle" type="button" popovertarget="site-nav" aria-label="Menu">
      <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" width="24" height="24" aria-hidden="true" focusable="false"><path fill="currentColor" d="M3 5h18v2H3zM3 11h18v2H3zM3 17h18v2H3z"/></svg>
    </button>
    <a class="luz-landing-header__brand" href="/">Acme Summit</a>
    <nav class="luz-navbar" id="site-nav" aria-label="Main" popover>
      <ul class="luz-navbar__list">
        <li><a class="luz-navbar__link" href="/programme/" aria-current="page">Programme</a></li>
        <li><a class="luz-navbar__link" href="/speakers/">Speakers</a></li>
        <li><a class="luz-navbar__link" href="/tickets/">Tickets</a></li>
      </ul>
    </nav>
    <div class="o-row luz-landing-header__actions">
      <a class="luz-btn luz-btn--ghost" href="/account/">Log in</a>
    </div>
  </div>
</header>
```

### Variants and options
There are no modifiers. The header is a class of the landing on a native `<header>`, laid out by core's objects in the markup.

- `.luz-landing-header`: On `<header>`: the page surface, a rule underneath, the gaps of its row, and the anchor its panels open under
- `.luz-landing-header__brand`: The site's name as a link to the home page: semibold, not underlined, at least 44 px tall; it takes the free room of the row
- `.luz-landing-header__actions`: On a `.o-row` at the end of the row: a search, a [language switch](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/site/lang-switch/), a button
- `.o-sticky` (core): Keeps the header at the top while the page scrolls, in a window at least 30 rem tall; see [the page and its bars](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/layout/#objects-page)
- `.o-container.o-container--inline.o-row` (core): The row: the width and gutters of the page, wrapping rather than overflowing
- `.luz-nav-toggle`, `.luz-navbar` (core): The menu button and the links: see the [navbar](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/navbar/)

### How it works
CSS from `@luz-ds/landing` on core's objects and navbar. No JavaScript, and `@luz-ds/site` is optional.

- The landing adds the skin only: the page surface, the rule underneath, the brand, and the gaps of the row (8 px between rows, 16 px between items, 24 px from 769 px). Core gives the rest: `.o-sticky` the stickiness and the scroll padding, `.o-container--inline` the gutters, `.o-row` the wrapping row, and the navbar the links and their panel.
- A one-row header is core's `--luz-bar-h` tall: 44 px controls, 4 px above and below, and the 1 px rule. With enlarged text the row wraps and the header grows.
- The header names itself the anchor `--luz-bar`, scoped to itself. Where the browser supports CSS anchor positioning, the navbar's panel and the list of site's `<luz-lang-switch>` open under it on one row or on two. Elsewhere they open at `--luz-bar-h` from the top of the window.
- Without `@luz-ds/site` nothing changes: its rules that refine site's elements match nothing.

### Without JavaScript
Nothing changes: the menu is a popover opened by the button's `popovertarget`, with no script, and the links are plain links.

### Keyboard and ARIA
- **Order:** the menu button, the brand, the links, then the actions, in the order of the source. With the menu open, the next Tab after the button goes into the panel's links.
- **Keys:** Enter or Space on the button opens and closes the panel; Escape closes it and returns focus to the button.
- **Names:** the `<nav>` has an `aria-label` ("Main"). The button's name is "Menu"; the browser exposes its expanded state. The current link has `aria-current="page"` and an underline.
- **Landmarks:** a `<header>` that is a direct child of `<body>` is the banner. Put the [skip link](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/skip-link/) before it.

### When to use
Use the header at the top of every page of a landing site: the visitor sees which site this is and reaches its main parts from any page.

### When not to use
Do not use it on a blog or a newspaper, or in an app: their packages have headers of their own.

- One header per page, never inside a component: it is the page's banner.
- A single page that fits one screen needs a heading and a skip link, not a header.

### Do and don't
- **Do** Three to six links, each a noun that names its part of the site, with the current one marked.
- **Don't** A dozen links, some of them vague: the row wraps into a wall and the visitor reads every word to choose.

### Writing the content
The brand is the site's name; the links are the names of its main parts.

- Brand: the name as people say it, one to three words. A logo is decorative: the name stays as text in the link.
- Links: three to six, one or two words each, the same words as the titles of the pages they go to. No "Home" beside a brand that already goes home.
- Actions: a verb that says what happens, such as "Log in". Menu button: "Menu", translated like the rest of the page.

## Hero
URL: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/landing/hero/
Example: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/examples/landing/hero.html
Files: .luz-landing-hero, __copy, __eyebrow, __title, __lead, __media · Package: @luz-ds/landing

Opens a home or landing page with its title, one sentence, the main actions and an optional picture.

### Known issues
None known.

### Copy the markup
Hero markup
```html
<section class="luz-landing-hero o-grid o-grid--split" aria-labelledby="hero-title">
  <div class="luz-landing-hero__copy">
    <p class="luz-landing-hero__eyebrow">12 and 13 May 2027 · Seville</p>
    <h1 class="luz-landing-hero__title" id="hero-title">Acme Summit 2027</h1>
    <p class="luz-landing-hero__lead">Two days of talks and workshops for retail teams.</p>
    <div class="o-actions">
      <a class="luz-btn luz-btn--primary" href="#register">Register</a>
      <a class="luz-btn luz-btn--outline" href="#programme">See the programme</a>
    </div>
  </div>
  <div class="luz-landing-hero__media">
    <div class="luz-image luz-image--4x3">
      <img src="/img/venue-1280.jpg" width="1280" height="960" alt="The main hall, full, before the opening talk" fetchpriority="high" decoding="async">
    </div>
  </div>
</section>
```

### Variants and options
There are no modifiers. The eyebrow, the lead and the picture are optional; with no picture the copy takes the whole width. The block is a class of the landing on core's split grid.

- `.luz-landing-hero`: On a `<section>` with core's `.o-grid.o-grid--split`: space above it, the gaps, and columns of at least 24rem (`--luz-grid-min`), so two equal columns when each gets 24rem, one below
- `.luz-landing-hero__copy`: The text and the actions, first in the source
- `.luz-landing-hero__eyebrow`: A short line above the title, in small capitals of the mono face; the sans in Arabic
- `.luz-landing-hero__title`: The title: heading font, 4xl size, balanced lines; 3xl below 1024 px and 2xl at 640 px and below
- `.luz-landing-hero__lead`: One or two sentences in the secondary text colour, 70 characters wide at most; xl, lg below 1024 px and base at 640 px and below
- `.luz-landing-hero__media`: The second column, holding core's [image frame](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/image/)

### How it works
A `<section>` named by its title, laid out by core's split grid and styled by `@luz-ds/landing`. No JavaScript, and `@luz-ds/site` is optional.

- The columns are core's [split grid](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/layout/#objects-actions), intrinsic: they follow the room the hero has, not the window. A hero as wide as the page splits from about 900 px of window; in a narrow column, or with larger text, it stays one column.
- The order is the source order: the copy comes first, on the left in a left-to-right page and on the right in a right-to-left one.
- The actions are core's [action group](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/layout/#objects-actions), `.o-actions`: at 640 px and below its buttons stack and take the whole width.
- The classes change the look only. The title must be the page's `<h1>`.

### Without JavaScript
Nothing changes: the hero is HTML and CSS.

### Keyboard and ARIA
The hero has no interaction of its own: Tab reaches its links in the order of the source.

- `aria-labelledby` on the `<section>` points at the title, so the hero is a region with the page's name.
- Keep it first inside `<main>`, so the skip link lands right before it.

### When to use
Use a hero at the top of a home page, a landing page or a front page, to say in a few words what the site or the event is and what to do first.

### When not to use
Do not use it on a page whose reader came to read or to do a task: use a plain `<h1>` and a lead paragraph, which are smaller.

- One hero per page, and only at the top.
- Not for a message in the middle of a page: use a [section](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/landing/section/), with core's [band](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/band/) if it must stand out.

### Do and don't
- **Do** One primary action, and a second one as an outline button.
- **Don't** Three primary buttons: the reader cannot tell which one comes first.
- **Do** A title that names the thing, and a lead that says what it gives the reader.
- **Don't** A slogan for a title, and a lead that repeats it without saying what it is.

### Writing the content
The title says what the site or the event is, in sentence case and in fewer than ten words.

- The eyebrow is a fact the reader needs at once (a date and a place, a product name), not a slogan. Leave it out if there is none.
- The lead is one or two short sentences: what the reader gets.
- Buttons start with a verb and say where they go: "Register", "See the programme".
- The picture's `alt` says what it shows, or is empty if it only decorates. It is the first thing on the page: no `loading="lazy"`.

## Main and sections
URL: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/landing/section/
Example: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/examples/landing/section.html
Files: .luz-landing-main, .luz-landing-section, .luz-landing-glow · Package: @luz-ds/landing

Gives a landing page its rhythm: wide room between the blocks of the main, a closer one inside each section, and an optional glow behind the page.

### Known issues
None known for the main and the sections. A section on core's [band](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/band/#known-issues) has the band's.

### Copy the markup
Main and sections markup
```html
<body class="o-page luz-landing-glow">
  <a class="luz-skip-link" href="#main-content">Skip to content</a>
  <!-- the header -->
  <main id="main-content" class="o-container o-stack luz-landing-main" tabindex="-1">
    <!-- the hero -->
    <section class="o-stack luz-landing-section" aria-labelledby="programme-title">
      <h2 id="programme-title">Programme</h2>
      <p>Twelve talks and six workshops over two days.</p>
    </section>
    <section class="o-stack luz-landing-section luz-band" aria-labelledby="last-seats-title">
      <h2 id="last-seats-title">Registration closes on 30 April</h2>
      <div class="o-actions">
        <a class="luz-btn luz-btn--primary" href="#register">Register now</a>
      </div>
    </section>
  </main>
  <!-- the footer -->
</body>
```

### Variants and options
Three classes of the landing, each on top of a core object. A section stands out on core's [band](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/band/).

- `.luz-landing-main`: On `main.o-container.o-stack`: 64 px (`--luz-space-3xl`) between the blocks and under the last one; none above the first, as the hero brings its own
- `.luz-landing-section`: On `section.o-stack`: 16 px (`--luz-space-md`) between its children
- `.luz-landing-glow`: On the `.o-page` element: the brand's subtle tint in the corner where reading starts, over a fade from the page surface to the muted one; none in print

### How it works
CSS from `@luz-ds/landing` on core's objects. No JavaScript, and `@luz-ds/site` is optional.

- Core's `.o-container` gives the main its width and gutters, and `.o-stack` the column; the landing's layer comes after core's objects, so its gaps win over the stack's.
- The glow's tint sits top left in a left-to-right page and top right in a right-to-left one: a gradient's position is physical, so the class flips it with `:dir(rtl)`.
- Use a section on a `<section>` when the group has its own heading, or on a `<div>` when it does not.

### Without JavaScript
Nothing changes: the main, the sections and the glow are CSS.

### Keyboard and ARIA
None of the three has an interaction or a role of its own.

- The `<main>` is the main landmark, and the target of the skip link: give it `id` and `tabindex="-1"`.
- A `<section>` named with `aria-labelledby` becomes a region landmark; name only the sections people would jump to.
- The glow carries no meaning: without it (forced colors, print) nothing is lost.

### When to use
Use the main and its sections for every page of a landing site, so the space between blocks is the same everywhere. Use the glow on a short page, such as a home page or a sign-up page, to give it some warmth.

### When not to use
Do not use a section to space the paragraphs of running text: the text styles already do.

- For blocks side by side, use core's [grid objects](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/layout/), such as `ul.o-grid.o-grid--split` for a few features of equal weight.
- Do not use the glow on a long page or behind a band: the tint competes with the band's.

### Do and don't
- **Do** Blocks of different kinds, spaced as one group: a heading, a lead, the content.
- **Don't** Running text in a section: every paragraph gets the section's gap, and the text reads as separate blocks.

### Writing the content
Start each section with a heading that says what the section is for.

- Use the next heading level after the page title: `<h2>` under the hero's `<h1>`.
- Keep one idea per section; a second idea is a second section.

## Footer
URL: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/landing/footer/
Example: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/examples/landing/footer.html
Files: .luz-landing-footer · Package: @luz-ds/landing

Ends every page of a landing site with who made it, its licence and a few secondary links, under a rule.

### Known issues
None known.

### Copy the markup
Footer markup
```html
<footer class="luz-landing-footer">
  <div class="o-container o-container--inline o-row">
    <p>Acme Inc. · MIT licence</p>
    <nav class="o-actions" aria-label="Links">
      <a class="luz-btn luz-btn--ghost luz-btn--sm" href="/status/">Service status</a>
      <a class="luz-btn luz-btn--ghost luz-btn--sm" href="/accessibility/">Accessibility statement</a>
    </nav>
  </div>
</footer>
```

### Variants and options
There are no modifiers. The footer is a class of the landing on a native `<footer>`, with a row of core's inside.

- `.luz-landing-footer`: On `<footer>`: a rule on top, 24 px above its row and 32 px below; its row spreads its children to the two ends, and is a column aligned to the start at 768 px and below
- `.o-container.o-container--inline.o-row` (core): The row: the width and gutters of the page, so its content starts where the main's does
- `.o-actions` (core): The links, as an [action group](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/layout/#objects-actions)

### How it works
CSS from `@luz-ds/landing` on core's objects. No JavaScript, and `@luz-ds/site` is optional.

- The landing adds the rule, the room around the row and how the row spreads its children; `.o-container--inline` lines the row up with the page's content.
- On an `.o-page` the main grows, so the footer rests on the bottom of a page shorter than the window.
- The column at 768 px and below does not wrap, so its children stay one under the other.

### Without JavaScript
Nothing changes: the footer is HTML and CSS. A [color mode switcher](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/mode-switcher/) inside it keeps working as radios.

### Keyboard and ARIA
The footer has no interaction of its own; its links keep theirs.

- A `<footer>` that is a direct child of `<body>` is the contentinfo landmark.
- Name a `<nav>` of links with `aria-label`, and keep the links in the same order on every page.

### When to use
Use the footer at the end of every page of a landing site, for who made it, its licence and a few secondary links.

### When not to use
Do not put the main navigation, or anything needed to finish a task, in the footer.

- Main navigation goes in the [header](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/landing/header/).

### Do and don't
- **Do** Two to four links that say where they go.
- **Don't** The main navigation in the footer: the reader has to reach the end of the page to move around.

### Writing the content
Keep it short: who made it, the licence, and two to four links.

- Each link says where it goes: "Accessibility statement", not "Legal".

## Landing page templates
URL: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/landing/templates/

The blocks of an event landing page to paste in and adapt, in the order a visitor reads them: hero, programme, speakers, tickets, call to action, registration and features.

This page is a library of whole-page templates: open its URL for the markup of each.

## CMS
URL: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/cms/

The page structure of a blog, a newspaper or any site of articles, from the header to the post listing, and how to tell whether you need it.

For one kind of site · @luz-ds/cms

The page structure of a blog, a newspaper or any site of articles, from the header to the post listing, and how to tell whether you need it.

A site of articles publishes many pages of the same shape: a story with its header, its text and its author, and lists that lead to them. This package holds the page structure of that kind of site: its header (a bar or a masthead), the page header, the article header with its table of contents, and the footer. The layout every page needs (the page, the sticky bar, the navbar) is core's, and the pieces that act for the whole site (search, language, cookie consent) are in [Site](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/site/).

- It works with any CMS and any stack. The classes go on any element, so a template of WordPress, Drupal, Ghost, Hugo or your own code can write them.
- Every class starts with `.luz-cms-`, uses semantic tokens only and sits in the cascade layer `luz.cms`, after site's. Each pattern is a class on a native element, laid out in the markup by core's objects.
- It has no script. Load `cms.css` after the CSS of tokens and core (and site's, if you use it): [Install LUZ](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/get-started/#site-kinds) has the command and the CDN tags. With core's script, the table of contents marks the section in view.
- It has a version of its own, 0.x while it grows, and needs version `^0.1.0` of tokens and core, declared as peer dependencies. Site is an optional peer: without it the patterns render the same, and the rules that refine site's elements match nothing.
- The post card, the post listing, related posts and the author box need no CSS of their own: they are core's card, avatar and pagination, put together on [CMS templates](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/cms/templates/).

### Use cms when

- You publish articles, posts or stories, each with a title, an author and a date.
- Your articles are long enough to need a table of contents beside the text.
- You want a header that names the publication and its sections, as a bar or as a newspaper's masthead.

### Use another package when

- Your site is a landing page: [Landing](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/landing/) has its header, hero and footer.
- Your pages are documentation or an app, with no author or date: core's [layout](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/layout/) and [navbar](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/navbar/) are the start.

## Header
URL: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/cms/header/
Example: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/examples/cms/header.html
Files: .luz-cms-header, __brand, __actions, --masthead, __top, __date, __sections · Package: @luz-ds/cms

Starts every page of a blog or a newspaper with the publication's name, its sections and a search: one row that stays at the top, or a masthead of three rows.

### Known issues
The header's own issues are those of the pieces of core it is made of, and one of the masthead.

- **The masthead's menu without anchor positioning.** In browsers without CSS anchor positioning, the sections menu of the masthead header opens near the top of the window and covers the publication name and the menu button while it is open. Escape, or a click outside the menu, closes it and returns to the page.
- **The menu panel.** If you keep pressing Tab after the last link of the open menu, focus moves on into the page and the menu stays open over it; Escape closes it. See the [navbar's known issues](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/navbar/#known-issues).
- **Sticky bar and enlarged text.** The scroll padding of `.o-sticky` is a minimum: at 300% text, with the bar wrapped to several rows, Safari can leave a field reached with Tab under it. Set `scroll-padding-block-start` on `html` to your header's real height, or leave out `.o-sticky`.

### Copy the markup
The blog bar, with site's search and language switch in its actions:

Blog bar markup
```html
<header class="luz-cms-header o-sticky">
  <div class="o-container o-container--inline o-row">
    <button class="luz-nav-toggle" type="button" popovertarget="cms-nav" aria-label="Sections">
      <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" width="24" height="24" aria-hidden="true" focusable="false"><path fill="currentColor" d="M3 5h18v2H3zM3 11h18v2H3zM3 17h18v2H3z"/></svg>
    </button>
    <a class="luz-cms-header__brand" href="/">The Vejer Review</a>
    <nav class="luz-navbar" id="cms-nav" aria-label="Sections" popover>
      <ul class="luz-navbar__list">
        <li><a class="luz-navbar__link" href="/news/" aria-current="true">News</a></li>
        <li><a class="luz-navbar__link" href="/culture/">Culture</a></li>
        <li><a class="luz-navbar__link" href="/opinion/">Opinion</a></li>
      </ul>
    </nav>
    <div class="o-row luz-cms-header__actions">
      <luz-search>…</luz-search>
      <luz-lang-switch>…</luz-lang-switch>
    </div>
  </div>
</header>
```

The masthead:

Masthead markup
```html
<header class="luz-cms-header luz-cms-header--masthead">
  <div class="o-container o-container--inline o-stack">
    <div class="o-row luz-cms-header__top">
      <p class="luz-cms-header__date"><time datetime="2026-10-14">Wednesday, 14 October 2026</time></p>
      <div class="o-row luz-cms-header__actions">
        <luz-search>…</luz-search>
      </div>
    </div>
    <a class="luz-cms-header__brand" href="/">The Vejer Review</a>
    <div class="o-row luz-cms-header__sections">
      <button class="luz-nav-toggle" type="button" popovertarget="cms-nav" aria-label="Sections">…</button>
      <nav class="luz-navbar" id="cms-nav" aria-label="Sections" popover>…</nav>
    </div>
  </div>
</header>
```

### Variants and options
One modifier. The header is a class of cms on a native `<header>`, laid out by core's objects in the markup.

- `.luz-cms-header`: On `<header>`: the blog bar. The page surface, a rule underneath, the gaps of its row, and the anchor its panels open under
- `.luz-cms-header--masthead`: The newspaper's masthead: three rows in an `.o-stack`, 16 px above and below, not sticky
- `.luz-cms-header__brand`: The publication's name as a link to the home page, in the heading font, semibold, underlined on hover only. In the bar it takes the free room of the row; in the masthead it is large and centred. A logo `<img>` inside it is 44 px tall in the bar, 88 px in the masthead
- `.luz-cms-header__actions`: On a `.o-row`: site's [search](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/site/search/), then its [language switch](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/site/lang-switch/)
- `.luz-cms-header__top`: Masthead only, on a `.o-row`: the date at the start and the actions at the end, on one row
- `.luz-cms-header__date`: Masthead only: today's date in a `<time datetime>`, small and secondary; it wraps to give the actions their room
- `.luz-cms-header__sections`: Masthead only, on a `.o-row`: the menu button and the navbar between two rules, centred from 769 px; its panel opens under this row
- `.o-sticky` (core): Keeps the blog bar at the top while the page scrolls, in a window at least 30 rem tall; see [the page and its bars](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/layout/#objects-page). Never on the masthead
- `.o-container.o-container--inline` (core): The width and gutters of the page, so the header starts where the content starts
- `.luz-nav-toggle`, `.luz-navbar` (core): The menu button and the sections: see the [navbar](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/navbar/)

### How it works
CSS from `@luz-ds/cms` on core's objects and navbar. No JavaScript, and `@luz-ds/site` is optional.

- cms adds the skin only: the page surface, the rule underneath, the brand, and the gaps of the row (8 px between rows, 16 px between items, 24 px from 769 px). Core gives the rest: `.o-sticky` the stickiness and the scroll padding, `.o-container--inline` the gutters, `.o-row` and `.o-stack` the rows, and the navbar the links and their panel.
- A one-row bar is core's `--luz-bar-h` tall: 44 px controls, 4 px above and below, and the 1 px rule. At 768 px and below the brand fills the room between the menu button and the actions and wraps there, so the controls stay on one row; with enlarged text the row wraps and the bar grows.
- The masthead is not sticky: three rows stuck to the top would take a third of a phone's screen. Its brand is 49 px from 1024 px, 39 px below and 31 px at 640 px and below (`--luz-text-4xl`, `-3xl` and `-2xl`, the steps of the landing hero).
- The bar, and in the masthead the sections row, name themselves the anchor `--luz-bar`, scoped to themselves. Where the browser supports CSS anchor positioning, the navbar's panel opens under them. Elsewhere it opens at `--luz-bar-h` from the top of the window (see Known issues).
- With `@luz-ds/site`, the list of its `<luz-lang-switch>` opens under the bar. Without it nothing changes: the rules that refine site's elements match nothing.
- The [table of contents](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/cms/toc/) of an article sticks under a bar with `.o-sticky`.

### Without JavaScript
Nothing changes: the menu is a popover opened by the button's `popovertarget`, with no script, the links are plain links, and site's search shows its link to the A–Z index.

### Keyboard and ARIA
- **Order:** the order of the source. In the bar: the menu button, the brand, the sections, then the actions. In the masthead: the actions of the top row, the brand, then the menu button and the sections.
- **Keys:** Enter or Space on the menu button opens and closes the panel; Escape closes it and returns focus to the button. The panel is not modal: Tab after its last link moves on.
- **Names:** the `<nav>` and the menu button are both named "Sections"; the browser exposes the button's expanded state. The section of an article has `aria-current="true"`, the section's own index `aria-current="page"`; both are underlined.
- **Brand:** a link, never a heading: the story's title is the page's one `h1`. A logo is an `<img>` whose `alt` is the publication's name, with no text beside it.
- **Landmarks:** a `<header>` that is a direct child of `<body>` is the banner. Put the [skip link](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/skip-link/) before it.

### When to use
Use the header at the top of every page of a blog or a newspaper: a reader who lands on a story from a search sees which publication it is and reaches its sections and its search.

- The blog bar for most sites: one row that stays at the top while the reader reads.
- The masthead for a newspaper's front page and sections, where the name and the date set the tone.

### When not to use
Do not use it on a landing page or in an app: their packages have headers of their own.

- One header per page, never inside a component or an article: it is the page's banner.
- Do not make the masthead sticky, and do not put the date in the bar: in one row it competes with the name.

### Do and don't
- **Do** The publication's name as text, and a few sections named as the reader knows them.
- **Don't** The name cut short with an ellipsis, or every tag of the site as a section: the reader cannot tell where they are.

### Writing the content
The brand is the publication's name; the sections are the names readers use for its parts.

- Brand: the name in full, as it appears on the publication. It wraps at a narrow width; never shorten it with an ellipsis.
- Sections: four to seven, one or two words each, the same words as the titles of their index pages.
- Date (masthead): written out in the language of the page, "Wednesday, 14 October 2026", with the same day in `datetime`.
- Menu button: "Sections", translated like the rest of the page.

## Page header
URL: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/cms/page-header/
Example: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/examples/cms/page-header.html
Files: .luz-cms-page-header, __title, __lead · Package: @luz-ds/cms

Gives a page that is not an article, such as About or Contact, its title and one sentence about what it is for.

### Known issues
None known.

### Copy the markup
Page header markup
```html
<div class="luz-cms-page-header">
  <h1 class="luz-cms-page-header__title">About the Review</h1>
  <p class="luz-cms-page-header__lead">An independent paper for Vejer and the coast, paid for by its readers.</p>
</div>
```

### Variants and options
There are no modifiers. The lead is optional.

- `.luz-cms-page-header`: The block, with 32 px of space below it
- `.luz-cms-page-header__title`: The title: heading font, 3xl size, light weight; 2xl at 640 px and below
- `.luz-cms-page-header__lead`: One paragraph in the secondary text colour, 600 px wide at most

### How it works
A wrapper with a title and a lead, styled by `@luz-ds/cms`. No JavaScript, and `@luz-ds/site` is optional.

- The classes change the look only. The title must be the page's `<h1>`.
- In Arabic the title has no letter-spacing, which would break the joins of the script.
- A story has the [article header](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/cms/article-header/) instead, with its section, standfirst and byline.

### Without JavaScript
Nothing changes: the page header is HTML and CSS.

### Keyboard and ARIA
The page header has no interaction.

- An `<h1>` title lets screen reader users find the page title from the heading list.
- Keep it inside `<main>`, so the skip link lands right before it.

### When to use
Use a page header at the top of a page of a blog or a newspaper that is not a story (About, Contact, a section's index) to give its title and one sentence about what it is for.

### When not to use
Do not use it for a section inside the page: use a plain heading of the right level.

- One page header per page.
- A story takes the [article header](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/cms/article-header/), which has its author and date.

### Do and don't
- **Do** A title of a few words and a lead that says what the reader can do here.
- **Don't** A title padded with words the reader skips, and a lead that says nothing new.

### Writing the content
The title names the page in a few words, in sentence case.

- The lead is one sentence, under 25 words, that says what the reader can do here.
- Match the title to the link that led here and to the start of `<title>`.

## Article header
URL: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/cms/article-header/
Example: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/examples/cms/article-header.html
Files: .luz-cms-article-header, __kicker, __title, __standfirst, __byline, __media · Package: @luz-ds/cms

Opens a story with its section, its title, a standfirst, who wrote it and when, and an optional lead picture.

### Known issues
None known.

### Copy the markup
Article header markup
```html
<header class="luz-cms-article-header">
  <p class="luz-cms-article-header__kicker"><a href="/coast/">Coast</a></p>
  <h1 class="luz-cms-article-header__title">What ten years of tide records say about the bay</h1>
  <p class="luz-cms-article-header__standfirst">Volunteers have read the gauge in the port twice a day since 2016. The sea is four centimetres higher, and winter storms now reach the old town's walls.</p>
  <div class="luz-cms-article-header__byline">
    <span class="luz-avatar luz-avatar--lg"><img src="/authors/ana-ruiz-96.jpg" width="48" height="48" alt=""></span>
    <div>
      <p>By <a href="/authors/ana-ruiz/">Ana Ruiz</a></p>
      <p class="luz-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-12">12 October 2026</time> <span>6 min read</span></p>
    </div>
  </div>
  <figure class="luz-cms-article-header__media">
    <div class="luz-image">
      <img src="/img/tide-gauge-1280.jpg" width="1280" height="720" alt="A green gauge post marked in centimetres, standing in shallow water by a stone quay" fetchpriority="high" decoding="async">
    </div>
    <figcaption>The tide gauge in the port, at low tide. Photo: Ana Ruiz.</figcaption>
  </figure>
</header>
```

### Variants and options
There are no modifiers. Only the title is required: leave out the parts you do not have.

- `.luz-cms-article-header`: The block: its parts one under another, 12 px apart, and 32 px of space below it
- `.luz-cms-article-header__kicker`: The section above the title, small capitals in the mono, like the eyebrow of the [hero](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/landing/hero/). Optional
- `.luz-cms-article-header__title`: The title: heading font, 3xl size, light weight, balanced lines; 2xl at 640 px and below
- `.luz-cms-article-header__standfirst`: One or two sentences in the secondary text colour, a size up from the body, 70 characters wide at most. Optional
- `.luz-cms-article-header__byline`: A row in the sans that wraps: an [avatar](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/avatar/), then the author and a [meta line](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/meta/) with the date. Optional
- `.luz-cms-article-header__media`: A `<figure>` with no panel around it, for an [image frame](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/image/) and its caption. Optional

### How it works
A grid with one column, styled by `@luz-ds/cms`, in its `cms.css`, loaded after `site.css`. No JavaScript.

- Each part styles its text through inheritance, so the class can go on the element that holds the text or on a wrapper around it. A CMS template that wraps the standfirst in a `<div>` works as well as a bare `<p>`. In a WordPress block template, give each block its class in `className`.
- The kicker is a link when your sections have pages, or plain text. The title must be the page's `<h1>`; the classes change the look only.
- The lead picture is the [image frame](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/image/) of core: it keeps its ratio and shows a flat surface until the picture loads. Do not set `loading="lazy"` on it: it is near the top of the page.
- A date the reader sees is a `<time>` with a machine-readable `datetime`. For a story updated after it was published, add a second line: `Updated <time datetime="…">…</time>`.

### Without JavaScript
Nothing changes: the article header is HTML and CSS.

### Keyboard and ARIA
The header has no interaction of its own: Tab reaches the kicker's and the author's links, in that order.

- The `<h1>` title lets screen reader users find the story from the heading list. The kicker comes before it in the source, as it does on the screen; it is short, so it does not delay the title.
- Inside an `<article>`, a `<header>` is not a landmark: no label is needed.
- An avatar beside the author's name is decorative: initials get `aria-hidden="true"`, a photo `alt=""`.

### When to use
Use an article header at the top of a story, a post or a report: a page with an author and a date, that people read from start to end.

### When not to use
Do not use it for a page with no author or date, such as a contact or a section page: use the [page header](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/cms/page-header/).

- For the first block of a home or a landing page, use the [hero](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/landing/hero/).
- For a story in a list, use a [post card](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/cms/templates/#post-card): the header is for the story's own page.

### Do and don't
- **Do** A title that says what happened, and a standfirst that adds what the title could not.
- **Don't** A title that hides the news, and a standfirst that repeats the title.
- **Do** A byline with the author's name as text and the date in words.
- **Don't** A photo with no name beside it, and a date only in numbers, which readers in other countries read in another order.

### Writing the content
The title says what happened or what the reader will learn, in sentence case, with no full stop. Keep it under 90 characters: lists and search results cut longer ones.

- The kicker is one or two words: the section, or the kind of piece ("Analysis", "Interview").
- The standfirst is one or two sentences, under 40 words, that add to the title. It is often the description the CMS shows in lists and in search engines.
- Write the date in words, with the month spelled out, in the reader's language. "6 min read" counts about 200 words a minute; leave it out on short posts.
- The caption says what the picture shows and who took it. The `alt` describes what someone who cannot see it needs; it never repeats the caption.

## Table of contents
URL: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/cms/toc/
Example: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/examples/cms/toc.html
Files: .luz-cms-article, __layout, .luz-cms-toc, __title, __list · Package: @luz-ds/cms

Lists the sections of a long article, beside the text when there is room and above it when there is not.

### Known issues
The mark on the section in view needs core's script; without it, no link is marked. Beside the text, the contents sit at the inline end but come first in the source, so Tab reaches them before the text. Not yet tested with a screen reader.

### Copy the markup
Table of contents markup
```html
<article class="luz-cms-article">
  <header class="luz-cms-article-header">…</header>
  <div class="luz-cms-article__layout">
    <nav class="luz-cms-toc" aria-labelledby="toc-title" data-luz-spy>
      <h2 class="luz-cms-toc__title" id="toc-title">Contents</h2>
      <ol class="luz-cms-toc__list">
        <li><a href="#method">How the readings were taken</a></li>
        <li><a href="#level">Four centimetres in ten years</a></li>
        <li><a href="#storms">Storms that reach the walls</a></li>
      </ol>
    </nav>
    <div class="luz-prose">
      <p>Since March 2016, a group of volunteers has read the tide gauge…</p>
      <h2 id="method">How the readings were taken</h2>
      <p>…</p>
      <h2 id="level">Four centimetres in ten years</h2>
      <p>…</p>
      <h2 id="storms">Storms that reach the walls</h2>
      <p>…</p>
    </div>
  </div>
</article>
```

### Variants and options
There are no modifiers. The contents are optional: without them, the text takes the first column alone.

- `.luz-cms-article`: The story: its width decides the layout, not the window's (a size container)
- `.luz-cms-article__layout`: The contents, then the text. When the article is 46rem wide or more: the text in the first column, the contents in a 13rem column at the inline end, 48 px apart; one column below that
- `.luz-cms-toc`: The `<nav>`. Beside the text it stays in view while the text scrolls, and a list taller than the window scrolls inside it
- `data-luz-spy` on `.luz-cms-toc`: Core's scroll spy marks the link of the section in view. Optional
- `.luz-cms-toc__title`: The heading of the contents, in the sans, semibold
- `.luz-cms-toc__list`: The list, with no markers and a rule along its inline start; one link a line
- `--luz-cms-toc-top`: The space above the contents while they stay in view: 24 px, or 24 px under a sticky bar (core's `.o-sticky`, one row of `--luz-bar-h`, such as the [header](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/cms/header/)). Set it on `.luz-cms-toc` for a header of another height

### How it works
A CSS grid inside a size container, from `@luz-ds/cms`. No JavaScript of its own.

- The layout follows the room the article has: in a page with a sidebar, or with larger text, the contents go above the text sooner. Below 46rem they are a plain list above the text, and do not stay in view: they would cover it.
- The contents come first in the source, so they are read first and Tab reaches them first, in both layouts. The text is one element, the second child of `__layout`; in a CMS, the element that holds the post's content.
- Each link points at the `id` of a section heading. Most CMSs can write those ids: in WordPress, the HTML anchor of each heading block.
- With core's script (`luz.js`, or `initSidebar()` from `@luz-ds/core/sidebar`), the link of the section in view gets `aria-current="true"`, which draws a bar and makes it semibold. The script finds the links by the `data-luz-spy` attribute on the `<nav>`: every link to a section of the page inside it.

### Without JavaScript
The contents are a list of links to the sections, which the browser scrolls to. Only the mark on the section in view needs the script; without it, no link is marked.

### Keyboard and ARIA
Tab moves through the links in order; Enter follows one. The browser moves focus and scrolls to the section.

- A `<nav>` named by its heading: screen reader users find it in the list of landmarks as "Contents". Use an `<ol>`: the sections have an order.
- `aria-current="true"` names the section in view; the script moves it. Without the script, nothing claims to be current.
- Under a sticky header, the scroll padding of core's `.o-sticky` keeps the section's heading clear of the header when a link is followed.

### When to use
Use a table of contents in an article of four or more sections, which people read in parts or come back to: a guide, a report, a long interview.

### When not to use
Do not use it in a short post: three paragraphs need no map.

- Not for links to other pages: that is navigation, in the [header](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/cms/header/) or a [sidebar](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/sidebar/).
- Not for the steps of a task done in order: number the steps in the text.

### Do and don't
- **Do** Section headings that say what each part is about, so the list reads as a summary.
- **Don't** Headings that could be in any article: the list tells the reader nothing.

### Writing the content
Each link is the text of its section's heading, word for word, so the reader recognises where it leads.

- List the `<h2>` of the article only. A list of more than about eight is a sign the article could be two.
- Call it "Contents", in the reader's language ("Contenido" in Spanish).

## Footer
URL: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/cms/footer/
Example: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/examples/cms/footer.html
Files: .luz-cms-footer · Package: @luz-ds/cms

Ends every page of a blog or a newspaper with who publishes it and a few secondary links, under a rule.

### Known issues
None known.

### Copy the markup
Footer markup
```html
<footer class="luz-cms-footer">
  <div class="o-container o-container--inline o-row">
    <p>The Vejer Review is published by a cooperative.</p>
    <nav class="o-actions" aria-label="Links">
      <a class="luz-btn luz-btn--ghost luz-btn--sm" href="/corrections/">Corrections</a>
      <a class="luz-btn luz-btn--ghost luz-btn--sm" href="/accessibility/">Accessibility statement</a>
    </nav>
  </div>
</footer>
```

### Variants and options
There are no modifiers. The footer is a class of cms on a native `<footer>`, with a row of core's inside.

- `.luz-cms-footer`: On `<footer>`: a rule on top, 24 px above its row and 32 px below; its row spreads its children to the two ends, and is a column aligned to the start at 768 px and below
- `.o-container.o-container--inline.o-row` (core): The row: the width and gutters of the page, so its content starts where the main's does
- `.o-actions` (core): The links, as an [action group](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/layout/#objects-actions)

### How it works
CSS from `@luz-ds/cms` on core's objects. No JavaScript, and `@luz-ds/site` is optional.

- cms adds the rule, the room around the row and how the row spreads its children; `.o-container--inline` lines the row up with the page's content.
- On an `.o-page` the main grows, so the footer rests on the bottom of a page shorter than the window.
- The column at 768 px and below does not wrap, so its children stay one under the other.

### Without JavaScript
Nothing changes: the footer is HTML and CSS. A [color mode switcher](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/mode-switcher/) inside it keeps working as radios.

### Keyboard and ARIA
The footer has no interaction of its own; its links keep theirs.

- A `<footer>` that is a direct child of `<body>` is the contentinfo landmark.
- Name a `<nav>` of links with `aria-label`, and keep the links in the same order on every page.

### When to use
Use the footer at the end of every page of a blog or a newspaper, for who publishes it and a few secondary links: corrections, contact, the accessibility statement.

### When not to use
Do not put the main navigation, or anything needed to finish a task, in the footer.

- The sections go in the [header](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/cms/header/).
- A landing page has a [footer](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/landing/footer/) of its own.

### Do and don't
- **Do** Two to four links that say where they go.
- **Don't** The main navigation in the footer: the reader has to reach the end of the page to move around.

### Writing the content
Keep it short: who publishes it, and two to four links.

- Each link says where it goes: "Accessibility statement", not "Legal".

## CMS templates
URL: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/cms/templates/

The pieces of a blog or a newspaper that need no CSS of their own, to paste in and adapt: the content page, the article page, a post card, post listings, related posts and the author box.

This page is a library of whole-page templates: open its URL for the markup of each.

## App
URL: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/app/

The header and the dashboard of a web application, on core's shell and sidebar, and how to tell whether you need them.

For one kind of site · @luz-ds/app

The header and the dashboard of a web application, on core's shell and sidebar, and how to tell whether you need them.

An application is used every day by the same people to check a state and act on one thing. The layout it needs is already core's: the shell with its sidebar, the drawer on a phone, the sticky bar, the grid and the card. This package holds the two pieces that only an application has: the bar at the top of the main area, with the search and the account, and the dashboard, a grid of panels under the view's title.

- Every class starts with `.luz-app-`, uses semantic tokens only and sits in the cascade layer `luz.app`, after site's, landing's and cms's. Each pattern is a class on a native element, laid out in the markup by core's objects.
- It has no script. Load `app.css` after the CSS of tokens and core (and site's, if you use its search): [Install LUZ](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/get-started/#site-kinds) has the command and the CDN tags. The sidebar is core's, with its own optional script.
- It has a version of its own, 0.x while it grows, and needs version `^0.1.0` of tokens and core, declared as peer dependencies. Site is an optional peer: without it the bar has no search, and everything else renders the same.
- There is no sidebar of its own: [core's sidebar](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/sidebar/) opens as a drawer at 768 px and below, with no script. An icon rail and a collapsible sidebar are not in 0.1.
- The app page, an empty dashboard and an app with no sidebar need no CSS of their own: they are markup to copy on [App templates](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/app/templates/).

### Use app when

- You build a tool that people sign in to, with a sidebar of sections and a view for each.
- You want a quiet bar for the global tools, and a dashboard of panels for the view's state.

### Use another package when

- Your site is a landing page or a blog: [Landing](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/landing/) and [CMS](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/cms/) have their headers.
- You only need a sidebar and a content area: core's [layout](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/layout/) and [sidebar](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/sidebar/) are enough.

## Header
URL: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/app/header/
Example: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/examples/app/header.html
Files: .luz-app-header, __product, __actions, __account, __account-name · Package: @luz-ds/app

The quiet bar at the top of an application's main area: the menu button, the product name on a phone, the search and the account.

### Known issues
The header's own issues are those of the pieces of core it is made of.

- **The account list without anchor positioning.** In browsers without CSS anchor positioning, the list opens as a sheet at the bottom of the window instead of under the button. Escape, or a click outside it, closes it.
- **Sticky bar and enlarged text.** The scroll padding of `.o-sticky` is a minimum: at 300% text, with the bar wrapped to several rows, Safari can leave a field reached with Tab under it. Set `scroll-padding-block-start` on `html` to your header's real height, or leave out `.o-sticky`.

### Copy the markup
The bar, in `.o-main` beside the sidebar, with site's search before the account:

App header markup
```html
<div class="o-shell">
  <nav class="luz-sidebar" id="app-nav" aria-label="Main" popover>…</nav>
  <div class="o-main">
    <header class="luz-app-header o-sticky">
      <div class="o-row">
        <button class="luz-nav-toggle" type="button" popovertarget="app-nav" aria-label="Menu">
          <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" width="24" height="24" aria-hidden="true" focusable="false"><path fill="currentColor" d="M3 5h18v2H3zM3 11h18v2H3zM3 17h18v2H3z"/></svg>
        </button>
        <p class="luz-app-header__product">Bodega</p>
        <div class="o-row luz-app-header__actions">
          <luz-search>…</luz-search>
          <div class="luz-dropdown">
            <button class="luz-btn luz-btn--ghost luz-app-header__account" type="button" popovertarget="account-menu"><span class="luz-avatar luz-avatar--sm">AM</span> <span class="luz-app-header__account-name">Ana Martín</span></button>
            <div class="luz-dropdown__menu" id="account-menu" popover>
              <ul class="luz-dropdown__list">
                <li><a class="luz-dropdown__item" href="/account/">Account settings</a></li>
                <li><a class="luz-dropdown__item" href="/logout/">Sign out</a></li>
              </ul>
            </div>
          </div>
        </div>
      </div>
    </header>
    <main class="luz-app-dashboard" id="main-content" tabindex="-1">…</main>
  </div>
</div>
```

### Variants and options
No modifier. The header is a class of app on a native `<header>`, laid out by core's objects in the markup.

- `.luz-app-header`: On `<header>`, a child of `.o-main`: the page surface and a rule underneath. It is one row of `--luz-bar-h`; its `.o-row` has the gutters of the content
- `.luz-app-header__product`: The product's name in medium text, semibold. It shows only at 768 px and below, where the sidebar is a drawer and its brand is out of sight
- `.luz-app-header__actions`: On a `.o-row`: the global tools at the inline end of the bar. Site's [search](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/site/search/), then the account
- `.luz-app-header__account`: On the `.luz-btn.luz-btn--ghost` that opens the account list: at least 44 by 44 px, with its initials in a `.luz-avatar` and then the name
- `.luz-app-header__account-name`: The account's name. At 640 px and below it is clipped to nothing, and stays in the button's name
- `.o-sticky` (core): Keeps the bar at the top while the page scrolls, in a window at least 30 rem tall; see [the page and its bars](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/layout/#objects-page)
- `.luz-dropdown` (core): The account list, a disclosure of links: see the [dropdown](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/dropdown/)

### How it works
CSS from `@luz-ds/app` on core's shell, sticky bar, drawer and dropdown. No JavaScript, and `@luz-ds/site` is optional.

- App adds the skin only: the page surface, the rule underneath and the gaps of the row (8 px between rows, 16 px between items). Core gives the rest: `.o-sticky` the stickiness and the scroll padding, `.o-row` the row, the nav toggle and the sidebar the drawer, and the dropdown the account list.
- A one-row bar is core's `--luz-bar-h` tall: 44 px controls, 4 px above and below, and the 1 px rule. With enlarged text the row wraps and the bar grows.
- The page is what scrolls, not `.o-main`, so the sticky bar stays at the window's top. If you give `.o-main` a height of its own and make it scroll, what it focuses stays clear of the bar through its scroll padding.
- The account list opens under its button and ends where the button ends, so it never leaves the window at the inline end of the bar.
- Without site there is no search: leave `<luz-search>` out. Nothing else changes.
- The view's `h1` and its main action are not here: they are the first row of the [dashboard](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/app/dashboard/). The bar holds only what is the same in every view.

### Without JavaScript
Nothing changes. The drawer and the account list are popovers opened by the button's `popovertarget`, with no script, and site's search shows its link to the A–Z index. In a browser without the popover API the sidebar stays in the page above the content, the menu button is not shown, and the account list stays under its button.

### Keyboard and ARIA
- **Order:** the order of the source and of the screen. Skip link, the sidebar (a column from 769 px), the search, the account, then the view. At 768 px and below the closed drawer is out of the order: skip link, menu button, search, account, then the view.
- **Keys:** Enter or Space on the menu button opens the drawer, and on the account button opens the list; Tab reaches each link in order; Escape closes it and returns focus to the button.
- **Names:** the menu button is named "Menu" (`aria-label`, translated like the rest of the page). The account button's name is its initials, then the name: "AM Ana Martín", so a person who says "click AM" finds it at any width. The browser exposes the buttons' expanded state.
- **Not a menu:** the account list is a list of links in a popover. It has no `role="menu"`, no `aria-haspopup` and no arrow keys.
- **Landmarks:** a `<header>` in `.o-main`, which is a `<div>`, is the page's banner, beside the `<main>`, never inside it. The sidebar is the one navigation, named "Main". Put the [skip link](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/skip-link/) first: it skips the sidebar and the bar.

### When to use
Use the header at the top of the main area of every view of an application: the person always finds the search and their account in the same place.

- One quiet row of global tools: the menu button, the search and the account.
- The product's name on a phone, where the sidebar's brand is behind the drawer.

### When not to use
Do not use it for the title of the view or for its actions: they go in the first row of the dashboard.

- One header per page, in `.o-main`: it is the page's banner.
- Do not put a primary button in the bar: the view's main action would be lost among the chrome.
- For a bar with the site's own sections, use the [navbar](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/navbar/) in the header of [landing](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/landing/header/) or [CMS](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/cms/header/).

### Do and don't
- **Do** Keep the bar to the tools that are the same in every view: the menu, the search and the account.
- **Don't** Put the view's main action next to the account: two things to press that are not alike, and the main one is lost among the chrome.

### Writing the content
The product is a name; the account is a person; the list holds what they can do about themselves.

- Product: the name as it appears in the sidebar's brand. Never shorten it: it wraps.
- Account: the person's name in full, and the initials of that name in the avatar. A photo has an empty `alt`, so the name is the button's name.
- List: two to four links, each a verb or a noun the person knows: "Account settings", "Sign out". Put "Sign out" last.
- Menu button: "Menu", translated like the rest of the page.

## Dashboard
URL: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/app/dashboard/
Example: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/examples/app/dashboard.html
Files: .luz-app-dashboard, __head, __title, __panel, __panel--wide · Package: @luz-ds/app

The view of an application at a glance: its title and main action, then a grid of panels that fills the room the view has.

### Known issues
None known.

### Copy the markup
The view: a title row, then the panels. The title row is a `<div>`, and each panel starts with its heading.

Dashboard markup
```html
<main class="luz-app-dashboard" id="main-content" tabindex="-1">
  <div class="luz-app-dashboard__head">
    <h1 class="luz-app-dashboard__title">Overview</h1>
    <div class="o-actions">
      <a class="luz-btn luz-btn--primary" href="/reports/new/">New report</a>
      <a class="luz-btn luz-btn--secondary" href="/export/">Export data</a>
    </div>
  </div>
  <ul class="o-grid o-grid--auto">
    <li class="luz-card luz-app-dashboard__panel luz-app-dashboard__panel--wide">
      <h2 class="luz-card__title">Sales this month</h2>
      <p class="luz-card__body">…</p>
    </li>
    <li class="luz-card luz-app-dashboard__panel">
      <h2 class="luz-card__title">Stock alerts</h2>
      <p class="luz-card__body">…</p>
    </li>
  </ul>
</main>
```

### Variants and options
One modifier, for the panel. The dashboard is a class of app on a native `<main>`; the grid and the card are core's.

- `.luz-app-dashboard`: On `<main>`: the view. 32 px of padding (16 px at 640 px and below), 24 px between its rows, and the container of its own size query
- `.luz-app-dashboard__head`: On a `<div>`: the title at the start and the actions at the end, on one row that wraps; at 640 px and below, a column
- `.luz-app-dashboard__title`: The view's one `<h1>`: 2xl size, semibold, in the text colour; xl at 640 px and below
- `.luz-app-dashboard__panel`: On a `.luz-card` in the grid: it can shrink, so a wide child never widens its column
- `.luz-app-dashboard__panel--wide`: Two columns, when the dashboard is at least 40 rem wide; one column below, so it never asks for a column that is not there
- `.o-grid.o-grid--auto` (core): On the `<ul>`: as many equal columns as fit, none narrower than 18 rem
- `.o-actions` (core): Two or three related actions: a row that wraps, a column of full-width actions at 640 px and below

### How it works
CSS from `@luz-ds/app` on core's grid and card. No JavaScript.

- The dashboard sets `--luz-grid-min: 18rem` for core's `.o-grid--auto`, so a column is never narrower than 18 rem and the number of columns follows the room: one at 320 px, two at 768 px, and three at 1280 px beside a sidebar.
- The dashboard is a size container. The wide panel asks how wide the dashboard is, not the window, so it fits with a sidebar and without one. From 40 rem two columns always exist (two of 18 rem and a gap), and at 200% text both are in rem, so it never overflows.
- The panels keep the order of the markup. There is no dense packing and no `order`: a wide panel that does not fit in what is left of a row starts the next one, and the gap stays. Reading order, focus order and what is drawn are the same.
- A panel can shrink, so a long line of code or a table inside it scrolls in its own wrapper and does not widen the column.
- Empty, loading and failed panels are the panel's own content: a sentence and a link, core's [progress](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/progress/) or [alert](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/alert/). There is no skeleton class in 0.1.

### Without JavaScript
Nothing changes: the grid, the container query and the cards are CSS.

### Keyboard and ARIA
- **Order:** the order of the source: the title row's actions, then each panel in turn. A panel that is a card with a link inside is reached by that link.
- **Headings:** the view has one `<h1>`, in the title row, and each panel starts with an `<h2>`. The title row is a `<div>`, not a `<header>`.
- **List:** the panels are a `<ul>` of `<li>`: a screen reader says how many there are. Safari can drop the list role from a list without markers; the headings still lead through the panels.
- **Actions:** an action that goes somewhere is a link (`<a href>`); one that does something on this page is a `<button type="button">`. Never an `<a>` without `href`.
- **Landmarks:** the dashboard is the page's `<main>`, the sibling of the [header](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/app/header/). It takes the skip link's target, with `tabindex="-1"`.

### When to use
Use the dashboard for a view that shows several things about the same subject, each short enough to read at a glance and each leading to its own page.

- An overview, a status page or a home view, where the person checks and then acts on one thing.
- The most important panel first, wide: it gets the room when the view has it.

### When not to use
Do not use it for a view that is one long thing: a table, a form or a document are not panels.

- One primary action per view, in the title row, never in a panel.
- Do not make a panel taller than its neighbours with row spans or dense packing: it moves a panel before the ones that come first in the markup.
- For a plain grid of cards in a page of content, use core's [grid](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/layout/#objects-grid) and [card](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/components/card/).

### Do and don't
- **Do** Put the title and the one main action in the first row, and one short thing in each panel, under its own heading.
- **Don't** Give every panel a primary button: the person cannot tell which thing to do first.

### Writing the content
The title names the view; each panel names one subject and says its state in a sentence.

- Title: a noun the person knows from the sidebar, "Overview", "Reports". The same words as the sidebar's link.
- Main action: a verb and what it makes, "New report". One per view.
- Panel title: the subject, "Stock alerts". Under it, one sentence with the number: "Three products are below their minimum."
- Link: where it goes, "Review stock", not "More" or "Click here".

## App templates
URL: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/app/templates/

The pieces of an application that need no CSS of their own, to paste in and adapt: the app page with its sidebar, an app with no sidebar and an empty dashboard.

This page is a library of whole-page templates: open its URL for the markup of each.

## Accessibility statement
URL: https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/accessibility/

LUZ aims for WCAG 2.2 level AA. What is checked on every change, what has not been tested, and the known issues. Last reviewed on 16 October 2026.

### Target

LUZ aims to meet [WCAG 2.2](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/) level AA, the level that EN 301 549 and the European Accessibility Act refer to.

A design system cannot make a service accessible by itself: how you use the components decides the result. Each component page says what is yours to do, under *Keyboard and ARIA* and *Writing the content*.

### What is checked on every change

- An automated scan with axe-core of the home page, in English, Spanish and Arabic, and of every page of the documentation, in the light, dark and high-contrast modes. On component and pattern pages the scan runs once with each tab open, and on a sample of pages once with the search dialog open, with results and with none. A serious or critical finding fails the build.
- Keyboard use of the sidebar drawer, the modal dialog, the tabs, the Code and Design tabs of the component pages, the "On this page" index, whose links open the tab of the section they point at, and the search: Ctrl+K, the arrow keys through the results, Enter and Escape.
- The pages with JavaScript turned off: content is readable at 320 pixels wide, the Code and Design sections of a component page show one after the other, the search button is a link to the A–Z index, and no control that needs JavaScript is left on screen doing nothing. The color mode switcher in the page footer shows as three radio buttons, which still set the mode. The language switch of the home page opens its list of languages, which are links, with the popover API and no script.
- Reduced motion: no transition or animation runs when the visitor asks for less motion.
- The timeline: its keys (arrows, Home and End on the dates, mirrored right to left), the Previous and Next buttons, the names of the buttons, that autoplay is opt-in with a visible Pause / Play button, and that with reduced motion autoplay never starts and the button is not shown.
- Forced colors: a focused button and a focused search result keep a visible outline, the selected tab keeps its underline, and the search dialog keeps its border.
- The home page in Arabic, right to left: it must not overflow at 320 pixels wide, with JavaScript or without it.
- Right-to-left text: the demo of every component, except the player, is laid out with `dir="rtl"` next to its left-to-right layout. Each element with text, and each control, must sit where the mirror image puts it, and nothing may overflow. The check runs with and without JavaScript.
- Contrast of the text written for the home and documentation pages, in all three modes.
- Before this release, the same automated suites ran once in Firefox 155 and in WebKit 26.6 and 27.2 (the engine of Safari), on Linux, and their findings were fixed. They do not run on every change, and neither is a test on macOS or iOS.
- `llms.txt` and `classes.json` are regenerated on every change; a stale one fails.
- Contrast of every token pair a component draws, by a script, in the three base modes. A theme of your own is measured by the same script, as [the themes page](https://nandovejer.github.io/luz/docs/tokens/themes/) shows.

### What has not been tested

- Screen readers. No assistive technology has been used to test this release: NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver, TalkBack and Orca have not been tried. Nothing here says a component works with them.
- Speech recognition and screen magnifier software.
- Right-to-left text by a person who reads it, or with a screen reader. Only the layout is measured by a script, and the player's controls are not part of that measurement.
- Zoom to 400 percent by hand. Only the 320 pixel width is measured.
- Research with disabled people.
- The accessibility reviewer that `@luz-ds/check` prints, and `luz-check` itself. They read source files and give advice; they do not open a page, measure on screen or use assistive technology. A run with no findings does not mean a page is accessible.

Automated tools find only part of the problems. Treat this list as the gap, and test your own pages.

### Known issues

- **Tooltip.** Escape does not close it. This partly fails WCAG 1.4.13 (Content on hover or focus). Keep tooltips non-essential.
- **Modal.** Its buttons use the `command` and `commandfor` attributes. In a browser without them, and without JavaScript, the open button does nothing.
- **Player.** MIDI needs JavaScript and Web Audio. Without them the player shows a message. On this documentation site, the example video's caption files load only with JavaScript; without it the browser lists the tracks but shows no text.
- **Select.** The open list is the browser’s or the system’s, so it looks and sounds different in each. Where the browser supports `appearance: base-select` (Chrome and Edge 135, Safari 27), LUZ styles the list too, and that list has not been tested with a screen reader yet. It works without JavaScript.
- **Linked card.** The link in the title covers the whole card, so the body text cannot be selected with a mouse. Keyboard selection, find in page and screen readers reach it as usual.
- **Table sorted in the browser.** The sorted column is exposed with `aria-sort` on its column header, and each sort is announced in a status message. Tabbing through the headings announces the column name; the sort state is read on the header cell and in the status message. Checked in the Chromium accessibility tree only; not yet tested with NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver, TalkBack or Orca.
- **Avatar with a photo.** If the photo does not load, the browser draws its text alternative inside the box, in capitals, and a long name can spill past it.
- **Code and Design tabs.** The tab you chose last opens after the page has loaded, so the content below the tabs can move once.
- **Find in page.** In browsers that do not support `hidden="until-found"` (Safari before 26.2, Firefox before 139), find in page (Ctrl+F) does not find text in the tab that is not open. In Safari 26.2 and later it opens the tab but does not scroll to the match. Open the other tab, or turn JavaScript off to see both.
- **Choose your snippet.** Without JavaScript the picker is not in the page, every snippet is shown one after the other, and the index table, whose cells are links to the snippets, is the navigation. With JavaScript the picker replaces the table and shows one snippet, and it announces the snippet shown through its `<output>`, a status message. The focus stays on the choice you made. That announcement has not been tested with a screen reader.
- **Make it yours, sizes demo.** The sizes demo is optional: the table of presets on the page lists the sizes without it. Without JavaScript the demo is not shown, so no control is left on screen doing nothing. With it, the sliders resize the page itself, not a sample, and the Reset sizes button puts the page back; nothing is stored, so a reload does the same. The size knobs change the text and the space of the page; a reader’s own text size is respected, because the scale is in rem and follows the browser’s text size.
- **Search shortcut.** Ctrl+K (⌘K on a Mac) opens the documentation search instead of the browser’s own web search box. Use the browser’s address bar to search the web. The shortcut is shown on the search button, does nothing while you type in a text area or editable content, and there is no single-key shortcut. In a one-line text field it still opens the search, so on a Mac it replaces Ctrl+K, “delete to the end of the line”, there. On a site that loads the search with `site.js`, the search’s own script loads when the page is idle, or when you point at or move to the search: a Ctrl+K pressed before that loads it and then opens the search, after a short wait on a slow connection. On a page without a search, Ctrl+K stays the browser’s.
- **Search.** It has not been tested with a screen reader. The number of results is announced once you stop typing. Until its script has loaded, the search is a link to the A–Z index, in the same place; if you are on that link when the script arrives, it stays until you leave it, and the focus is never moved. If the script cannot load, the link stays. Closing the search returns the focus to where it was; if nothing had the focus, as after Ctrl+K on a page just loaded, it goes to the search button, and the next Tab continues from there.
- **Search at 400 percent zoom.** The whole search dialog scrolls, so the search field can move out of view while you read the results. Shift+Tab or the Up arrow from the first result brings you back to it.
- **Language switcher.** The list of languages opens at a fixed place under the header, not next to its button. Below 360 pixels wide its button shows a globe only; the language’s name is still the button’s accessible name. It has not been tested with a screen reader.
- **Navbar menu.** On narrow screens the menu of a navbar, in a landing, CMS or docs header, opens as a panel under the header. If you keep pressing Tab after its last link, focus moves into the page and the panel stays open over it. Press Escape to close it. (WCAG 2.2 success criterion 2.4.12, level AAA; level AA 2.4.11 is met.) Where CSS anchor positioning is supported (Chrome and Edge 125, Safari 26, Firefox 147) the panel opens under the header wherever it ends. In older browsers it opens at the height of a one-row bar at the default text size (`--luz-bar-h`), from the top of the window: with enlarged text and a header that wraps to a second row, or with a banner above the header before the page scrolls, it can cover part of the header.
- **Submenu.** A submenu of a header’s links is a native disclosure: Escape and a click outside do not close it; its own button or opening another one does (several can stay open in Firefox before 130 and Safari before 17.2). From 769 pixels wide an open submenu stays over the top of the page, so if you keep pressing Tab after it, a link behind it can be hidden (WCAG 2.2 success criterion 2.4.11, Focus not obscured, minimum). Press its button to close it. In the narrow menu its links are in the flow and Escape closes the whole menu. It has not been tested with a screen reader.
- **Banner.** It cannot be closed. It has no script.
- **Cookie consent.** Without JavaScript the banner is not shown, because none of the site's own scripts run either; the cookie policy is a link on every page. With it, the banner shows as a band fixed at the bottom of the window, so nothing on the page moves; it comes first after the skip link in the reading and Tab order, takes no focus when the page loads, does not block the page, and Escape neither answers nor hides it. While it shows, the page keeps room for it at its end and scrolls what Tab reaches above it (WCAG 2.2 success criterion 2.4.11); in Safari, which ignores that scroll padding for text fields, a script scrolls a field reached with Tab back above the band. In a window less than 30 rem tall it is in the flow at the top of the page instead, so the page moves down when it appears. Its confirmation hides with its Close button, which returns focus to the button that opened the banner or to the main content, or when focus leaves it for the page; a click on an empty part of the page does not hide it. The answer is stored in the browser, not in a cookie. It has not been tested with a screen reader.
- **Auto color mode.** The `<luz-mode>` element adds an Auto radio to the color mode switcher. Without JavaScript the four radios still change the mode, but Auto is light: the system setting and the time of day are followed only by the script. Where the page does not have the small script for the head, a page that follows a dark system can paint light first. With `by="clock"` Auto is dark from 20:30 to 07:30 even when the device is set to light. With `prefers-contrast: more` and a dark setting, Auto gives the high-contrast mode. The cycle button says Auto, not the mode applied. It has not been tested with a screen reader.
- **Sticky header, enlarged text.** A sticky header (`.o-sticky`) keeps a field reached with Tab clear of it by a minimum height. That works at 100 and 200 percent text. At 300 percent text, when the header wraps to several rows, Safari can still leave the field partly under it; Chrome, Edge and Firefox keep it clear. The Layout objects page and the landing and CMS Header pages say how to set the padding for your own header. In Firefox with forced colors the dim layer behind the open menu is not drawn; the panel keeps its border.
- **Band.** A band (`.luz-band`) cuts off whatever sticks out of it above or below, so a tooltip on the first control of a band is clipped at 200 percent text and larger; start the band with its heading. The hover of an outline or ghost button on a band shows no change. In forced colors the band has no tint, only two thin rules above and below it.
- **Prose.** A table that is wider than the text column and has no `.luz-table-wrap` around it makes the whole page scroll sideways on a narrow screen. A long preformatted block scrolls inside itself; give it `tabindex="0"` and a name, as the code block has, or Safari users cannot scroll it with the keyboard.
- **Meta line.** The dots between the facts are hidden from screen readers with alternative text for generated content. In a browser without it (Firefox before 128, Safari before 17.4) a screen reader reads each dot.
- **Lists laid out as a grid, stack or row.** Safari does not announce a list whose markers are removed, outside a navigation landmark, as a list. Its items are still read in order, and the headings in them still lead through it.
